---
<!-- maintheorem-1: body_md -->
Let \((V,0)\) be a normal \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein complex surface singularity. Put
 
\[
 \varepsilon(V,0)=
 \begin{cases}
 1&\text{if \((V,0)\) is Gorenstein},\\
 0&\text{if \((V,0)\) is non-Gorenstein}.
 \end{cases}
\]
 
If \((V,0)\) is not a rational double point, then
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)\geq\varepsilon(V,0),
\]
 
with equality if and only if \((V,0)\) is quasi-homogeneous. For a rational double point, \(\Delta(V,0)=0\).
<!-- end maintheorem-1 -->
<!-- maintheorem-2: body_md -->
Let \(\pi\) be a one-parameter smoothing of a rational normal complex surface singularity with local ring \(A\) and canonical index \(r>1\). Let \(n\) be the number of exceptional components of its minimal good resolution and \(K\) its numerical canonical cycle. There are rational numbers \(\gamma_i(A)\), depending only on \(A\), such that
 
\[
 \delta_i(\pi)=\binom{i}{2}(\mu_\pi-n-K^2)+\gamma_i(A)
 \quad(i\in\mathbb{Z}).
\]
 
They satisfy
 
\[
 \gamma_{i+r}(A)=\gamma_i(A),\quad
 \gamma_i(A)=\gamma_{1-i}(A),\quad
 \gamma_0(A)=\gamma_1(A)=0.
\]
<!-- end maintheorem-2 -->
<!-- maintheorem-3: body_md -->
Every rational homology disk smoothing \(\pi\) of a normal complex surface singularity \((V,0)\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. Its central singularity is rational and weighted homogeneous, and
 
\[
 \tau_\pi=1,\quad \alpha_\pi=0,\quad \Delta(V,0)=0.
\]
<!-- end maintheorem-3 -->
<!-- remark--1: body_md -->
Beke--Park--Shin--Stipsicz~\cite{BPSS2026} prove that a normal complex surface singularity whose minimal good resolution graph has at least two nodes admits no rational homology disk smoothing. Their proof combines Wahl's formula for the dimension of a rational homology disk smoothing component with estimates for logarithmic cohomology on the resolution. Together with the known classification in the quasi-homogeneous case, this yields the same complete classification.
<!-- end remark--1 -->
<!-- maintheorem-4: body_md -->
Let \((V,0)\) be a normal complex surface singularity which is not a rational double point. For every holomorphic function \(f\colon(V,0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)\) defining a reduced curve and having an isolated critical point at the origin,
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)=1+j_f-\mu_f.
\]
<!-- end maintheorem-4 -->
<!-- maintheorem-5: body_md -->
For every normal complex surface singularity \((V,0)\),
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)+4p_g(V,0)\geq0,
\]
 
with equality if and only if \((V,0)\) is rational and quasi-homogeneous.
<!-- end maintheorem-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:index}
Let \((V,0)\) be a normal complex surface singularity which is not a rational double point. For every holomorphic function \(f\colon(V,0) \to (\mathbb{C},0)\) defining a reduced curve and having an isolated critical point at the origin,
 
\begin{equation*}                 
 \Delta(V,0)=1+j_f-\mu_f.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:resolution-comparison}
With the above notation, one has
 
\[
 H^0(\widetilde{X},S_{\widetilde{X}})=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}} A
\]
 
and
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:correction}
 \Delta(V,0) = \Delta_{\widetilde{X}}+a_{\widetilde{X}}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
\emph{Lifting vector fields.} Every derivation of \(A\) preserves \(\mathfrak{m}_A\) and lifts uniquely to a logarithmic vector field on the minimal good resolution; see Bergner--Graf~\cite[\S2, Fact~1 and Proposition~1]{BergnerGraf2020}. We show that these vector fields lift through \(q\).

On an intermediate resolution \(Y\), write locally
 
\[
\mathfrak{m}_A\mathcal{O}_Y=gJ,
\]
 
where \((g)\) is the fixed divisorial part and \(J\) is the residual ideal. A lifted derivation \(\delta\) preserves \(gJ\), and logarithmicity gives \(\delta(g) \in (g)\). Hence
 
\[
\delta(J) \subseteq J.
\]
 
In characteristic zero, the radical of a derivation-invariant ideal is also invariant. At each residual base point \(y\), we have \(\sqrt{J_y}=\mathfrak{m}_y\), and therefore
 
\[
\delta(\mathfrak{m}_y^k) \subseteq \mathfrak{m}_y^k
\quad\text{for all } k \ge 0.
\]
 
Thus \(\delta\) induces a graded derivation of the Rees algebra and lifts to the blowup at \(y\), logarithmically along the reduced total exceptional divisor. Induction proves that every derivation of \(A\) lifts through \(q\). Conversely, a vector field on \(Y\) acts on \(H^0(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y)=A\). Consequently,
 
\[
H^0(\widetilde{X},S_{\widetilde{X}})
=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}} A.
\]
 
The same argument applies to every intermediate resolution; in particular, all global logarithmic vector fields vanish at each subsequent blowup center.

\emph{Change under a point blowup.} Use the analogous notation \(S_Y,L_Y,a_Y,\Delta_Y\) on each intermediate resolution. Consider a blowup \(b\colon Y' \to Y\) at a smooth point \(y\) of the reduced exceptional divisor \(D\), and let \(F\) be its exceptional curve. By Flenner--Zaidenberg~\cite[Lemma~1.5(3)]{FlennerZaidenberg1994},
 
\[
0 \to b_*S_{Y'} \to S_Y \to T_yD \to 0,
  R^1b_*S_{Y'}=0,
\]
 
where \(T_yD\) is viewed as a skyscraper sheaf. The evaluation map on global sections is zero by the preceding paragraph, so
 
\[
h^1(S_{Y'})=h^1(S_Y)+1.
\]
 
Moreover,
 
\[
L_{Y'} \simeq b^*L_Y(-F),
  b_*L_{Y'}=L_Y\mathfrak{m}_y,
  R^1b_*L_{Y'}=0.
\]
 
Put
 
\[
c=\operatorname{rank}(
H^0(Y,L_Y) \to L_Y|_y
).
\]
 
The evaluation sequence for \(L_Y\) gives
 
\[
h^1(L_{Y'})=h^1(L_Y)+1-c,
  a_{Y'}=a_Y+c.
\]
 
Since \(h^1(\mathcal{O}_{Y'})=h^1(\mathcal{O}_Y)\), it follows that
 
\[
\Delta_{Y'}+a_{Y'}=\Delta_Y+a_Y.
\]

If the center is a node of \(D\), then \(S_{Y'} \simeq b^*S_Y\) by Flenner--Zaidenberg~\cite[Lemma~1.5(4)]{FlennerZaidenberg1994}, and \(L_{Y'} \simeq b^*L_Y\). Thus both \(\Delta_Y\) and \(a_Y\) remain unchanged. Applying these observations along \(q\), and using \(a_X=0\) from \eqref{eq:anti}, yields
 
\[
\Delta_{\widetilde{X}}+a_{\widetilde{X}}
=\Delta(V,0). \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:function-conservation}
For general sufficiently small \(t \neq 0\), one has
 
\[
j_f-\mu_f=j_{f_t}-\mu_{f_t}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We show that both \(j_f\) and \(\mu_f\) decrease by the sum of the Milnor numbers at the critical points of \(f_t\) away from the origin. For \(j_f\), we prove flatness of the relative Jacobian quotient; for \(\mu_f\), we use conservation of the radial index.

Set \(T=\mathbb{C}\{t\}\), \(R=A\{t\}\), and
 
\[
\mathscr{D}=(\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}} A)\otimes_A R,
 \mathscr{Q}=R/df_t(\mathscr{D}),
\]
 
Here \(df_t\) denotes differentiation along \(V\), and \(\mathscr{Q}\) is the relative Jacobian quotient. The modules \(\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}} A\) and \(\omega_A^\vee\) are reflexive over the normal local ring \(A\), hence maximal Cohen--Macaulay. Their extensions to the normal three-dimensional algebra \(R\) therefore have depth three. Since
 
\[
\mathscr{Q}/t\mathscr{Q} \simeq A/J_f
\]
 
has finite length, the analytic finiteness theorem implies that \(\mathscr{Q}\) is finite over \(T\).

The image of \(df_t\colon\mathscr{D} \to R\) is torsion-free, so the localized depth lemma shows that its kernel is reflexive. Outside the singular axis and \(\operatorname{Supp}\mathscr{Q}\), contraction with \(df_t\) identifies this kernel with \(\omega_A^\vee\otimes_A R\). Both excluded sets have codimension at least two. Reflexive extension therefore gives an exact sequence
 
\[
0 \to \omega_A^\vee\otimes_A R
 \to \mathscr{D}
 \xrightarrow{df_t} R
 \to \mathscr{Q} \to 0.
\]
 
Applying the depth lemma twice yields
 
\[
\operatorname{depth}_R\mathscr{Q} \ge 1.
\]
 
The \(T\)-torsion submodule of \(\mathscr{Q}\), if nonzero, would be finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb{C}\), since \(\mathscr{Q}\) is finite over \(T\). It would thus be a nonzero finite-length \(R\)-submodule, contrary to the positive depth of \(\mathscr{Q}\). Hence \(\mathscr{Q}\) is finite free over \(T\), of rank \(j_f\).

Choose sufficiently small representatives on which the corresponding quotient sheaf is finite over the parameter disc. After shrinking the disc, its direct image is locally free of rank \(j_f\). Let \(\Sigma_t\) be the set of critical points of \(f_t\) away from the origin in the chosen representative. For \(p \in \Sigma_t\), the surface \(V\) is smooth at \(p\), and the local quotient has length
 
\[
\dim_{\mathbb{C}}
\frac{\mathcal{O}_{V,p}}{df_t(\Theta_{V,p})}
=\mu(f_t,p),
\]
 
where \(\mu(f_t,p)\) is the Milnor number of \(f_t-f_t(p)\) at \(p\). Constancy of the total fiber length gives
 
\[
j_f=j_{f_t}+\sum_{p \in \Sigma_t}\mu(f_t,p).
\]

By Ebeling--Gusein-Zade--Seade~\cite[Remark~2.4 and Example~2.6]{EbelingGuseinZadeSeade2004}, the radial index of \(df\) on the complex surface \(V\) equals \(1-\chi(F_f)=\mu_f\) and satisfies conservation of number. At each \(p \in \Sigma_t\), the radial index of \(df_t\) equals \(\mu(f_t,p)\). Consequently,
 
\[
\mu_f=\mu_{f_t}+\sum_{p \in \Sigma_t}\mu(f_t,p).
\]
 
Subtracting the two identities proves
 
\[
j_f-\mu_f=j_{f_t}-\mu_{f_t}. \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:logarithmic-differential}
Let \(f \in \mathfrak{m}_A\) define a reduced curve and have an isolated critical point at the origin.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Let \(r\colon(Y,D) \to (V,0)\) be a good resolution, and put \(S_Y=\Theta_Y(-\log D)\) and \(L_Y=\mathcal{O}_Y(-(K_Y+D))\). Suppose that
 
\[
 \operatorname{div}_Y(f)=Z+H,\quad
 Z=\sum_i z_iD_i,\quad z_i>0,
\]
 
where \(D=\sum_iD_i\) is the reduced exceptional divisor and \(H\) is smooth, reduced, transverse to \(D\), and disjoint from its nodes. On a sufficiently small representative, there is an exact sequence
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:df}
 0 \to L_Y(Z) \to S_Y \xrightarrow{df} \mathcal{O}_Y(-Z) \to 0.
\end{equation}

\item For the principalization \(\widetilde{p}\colon(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{E}) \to (V,0)\) fixed above, if the image of \(f\) in \(\mathfrak{m}_A/\mathfrak{m}_A^2\) is sufficiently general, the hypotheses of \textup{(i)} hold with \((Y,D,Z)=(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{E},M)\). Moreover,
 
\[
 H^0(\widetilde{X},\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-M))=\mathfrak{m}_A,
 \quad
 H^0(\widetilde{X},L_{\widetilde{X}}(M)) \simeq \omega_A^\vee.
\]
 
The second identification agrees with restriction away from \(\widetilde{E}\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
(i) Logarithmic vector fields preserve the ideal of every component of \(D\), so differentiation gives \(df\colon S_Y \to \mathcal{O}_Y(-Z)\). We check surjectivity along \(D\). At a smooth point of \(D\) outside \(H\), write \(D=\{x=0\}\) and \(f=x^mu\), where \(u\) is a unit. In the basis \(x\partial_x,\partial_y\), the normalized map is
 
\[
 x^{-m}df=(mu+xu_x,u_y).
\]
 
The first coefficient restricts to the unit \(mu\) on \(x=0\). At a point of \(D\cap H\), choose coordinates with \(f=x^my\). Then
 
\[
 x^{-m}df=(my,1).
\]
 
At a node, write \(D=\{xy=0\}\) and \(f=x^my^nu\), where \(u\) is a unit. In the basis \(x\partial_x,y\partial_y\), the map is
 
\[
 x^{-m}y^{-n}df=(mu+xu_x,nu+yu_y).
\]
 
Both coefficients are nonzero at the node. Away from \(D\), surjectivity follows because \(f\) has no critical point on \(V\setminus\{0\}\), after shrinking the representative. The kernel is therefore invertible, and taking determinants gives
 
\[
 \ker(df) \simeq \det(S_Y)\otimes\mathcal{O}_Y(Z)=L_Y(Z).
\]
 
This proves \eqref{eq:df}.

(ii) Write \(f=g+h\), where \(g\) is a general linear combination of fixed minimal generators of \(\mathfrak{m}_A\) and \(h \in \mathfrak{m}_A^2\). Their pullbacks generate \(\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-M)\). Thus
 
\[
 \operatorname{div}_{\widetilde{X}}(g)=M+H_g,
\]
 
where, near \(\widetilde{E}\), the divisor \(H_g\) is smooth, reduced, transverse to \(\widetilde{E}\), and disjoint from its nodes. Let \(s\) be a local equation of \(M\). Since \(h \in \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-2M)\), we may write
 
\[
 g=su,\quad h=s^2v,\quad f=s(u+sv).
\]
 
All coefficients of \(M\) are positive, so
 
\[
 \left.\frac{f}{s}\right|_{\widetilde{E}}
 =\left.\frac{g}{s}\right|_{\widetilde{E}}.
\]
 
These restrictions have the same simple zeros on each exceptional component and do not vanish at a node. At each zero, the tangent derivative along that component is nonzero. Hence the divisor of \(f/s\) is smooth and transverse there. After shrinking the representative, we obtain \(\operatorname{div}_{\widetilde{X}}(f)=M+H\) with the required properties.

Normality gives \(H^0(\widetilde{X},\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}})=A\). Since \(M \ge \widetilde{E}\),
 
\[
 \mathfrak{m}_A
 \subseteq H^0(\widetilde{X},\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-M))
 \subseteq \{a \in A:a(0)=0\}=\mathfrak{m}_A.
\]
 
The first inclusion follows from the definition of \(M\), proving the first identification.

Put \(\mathscr{K}_f=\ker(df\colon\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}} A \to A)\). As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:function-conservation}, the depth lemma shows that \(\mathscr{K}_f\) is reflexive: \(\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}} A\) has depth two and its image \(J_f\) is torsion-free. On \(U=V\setminus\{0\}\), contraction gives the isomorphism
 
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \omega_U^\vee \simeq \bigwedge\nolimits^2\Theta_U
 & \to \ker(df\colon\Theta_U \to \mathcal{O}_U),\\
 v\wedge w& \mapsto df(v)w-df(w)v.
 \end{aligned}
\]
 
Reflexive extension identifies \(\mathscr{K}_f\) with \(\omega_A^\vee\). Taking sections in \eqref{eq:df} and using Lemma~\ref{lem:resolution-comparison}, we obtain
 
\[
 H^0(\widetilde{X},L_{\widetilde{X}}(M))
 \simeq \mathscr{K}_f \simeq \omega_A^\vee.
\]
 
The identifications agree with restriction away from \(\widetilde{E}\).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:milnor-cycle}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:logarithmic-differential}\textup{(i)}, put \(D_i^\circ=D_i\setminus ((D-D_i)\cup H)\). Then
 
\[
 \chi(F_f)=\sum_i z_i\chi(D_i^\circ)
 =Z^2-(K_Y+D)\cdot Z.
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let \(g_i\) be the genus of \(D_i\), and set
 
\[
 t_i
 =
 (D-D_i)\cdot D_i.
\]
 
All intersections are transverse, and \(H\) avoids the nodes. Therefore
 
\[
 \chi(D_i^\circ)
 =
 2-2g_i-t_i-H\cdot D_i.
\]

Choose disjoint small discs around the deleted points on each \(D_i\). Over the resulting compact core of \(D_i^\circ\), the local equation \(f=x^{z_i}u\), with \(u\) a unit, identifies the nearby fiber with an unramified covering of degree \(z_i\). Its Euler characteristic is thus \(z_i\chi(D_i^\circ)\).

At a node \(D_i\cap D_j\), the local equation can be written, after absorbing a unit into a coordinate, as
 
\[
 x^{z_i}y^{z_j}=\varepsilon.
\]
 
Its intersection with a sufficiently small bidisc consists of \(\gcd(z_i,z_j)\) annuli. At a point of \(D_i\cap H\), the corresponding equation is
 
\[
 x^{z_i}y=\varepsilon,
\]
 
which gives one annulus. The remaining boundary pieces are collars, and all these pieces have Euler characteristic zero. They are attached along boundary circles, whose Euler characteristic is also zero. Additivity therefore gives
 
\[
 \chi(F_f)
 =
 \sum_i z_i\chi(D_i^\circ)
 =
 \sum_i z_i
 (2-2g_i-t_i-H\cdot D_i).
\]

Adjunction on each exceptional component gives
 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 (K_Y+D)\cdot D_i
 &= (K_Y+D_i)\cdot D_i +(D-D_i)\cdot D_i\\
 &=2g_i-2+t_i.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
 
Moreover, \(Z+H\) is the divisor of a function, so
 
\[
 (Z+H)\cdot D_i=0
\]
 
for every \(i\). Multiplying by \(z_i\) and summing yields
 
\[
 Z^2+H\cdot Z=0.
\]
 
Consequently,
\begin{align}\label{eq:milnor}
 \chi(F_f)
 &=
 \sum_i z_i
 (2-2g_i-t_i-H\cdot D_i)\notag\\
 &=
 -(K_Y+D)\cdot Z-H\cdot Z\notag\\
 &=
 Z^2-(K_Y+D)\cdot Z.
\end{align}
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Recall that \(A=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}\) and \(\Delta(A)=\Delta(V,0)\). By Lemma~\ref{lem:function-conservation}, replacing \(f\) by \(f+t\ell\) for general sufficiently small \(t\) does not change \(j_f-\mu_f\). We may therefore assume that its image in \(\mathfrak{m}_A/\mathfrak{m}_A^2\) is sufficiently general. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:logarithmic-differential}\textup{(ii)} to the chosen principalization \(\widetilde{X} \to X\). We compute \(\Delta_{\widetilde{X}}+a_{\widetilde{X}}\) from the cohomology sequence of \eqref{eq:df} and two restriction sequences.

Write \(p_g=h^1(\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}})\) for the geometric genus of \((V,0)\). Using the vanishing of \(H^2\), the cohomology sequence of \eqref{eq:df} gives
 
\[
 0 \to \mathfrak{m}_A/J_f
 \to H^1(\widetilde{X},L_{\widetilde{X}}(M))
 \to H^1(\widetilde{X},S_{\widetilde{X}}) \to H^1(\widetilde{X},\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-M))
 \to 0.
\]
 
Since \(\dim_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathfrak{m}_A/J_f)=j_f-1\), it follows that
 
\[
 h^1(S_{\widetilde{X}})
 =
 h^1(L_{\widetilde{X}}(M))+h^1(\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-M))-(j_f-1).
\]

Next, consider the restriction sequence
 
\[
 0 \to L_{\widetilde{X}}
 \to L_{\widetilde{X}}(M)
 \to L_{\widetilde{X}}(M)|_M
 \to 0.
\]
 
The identification of \(H^0(L_{\widetilde{X}}(M))\) in Lemma~\ref{lem:logarithmic-differential} gives the cohomology sequence
 
\begin{multline*}
 0
 \to 
 \omega_A^\vee/H^0(\widetilde{X},L_{\widetilde{X}})
 \to H^0(M,L_{\widetilde{X}}(M)|_M)
 \to H^1(\widetilde{X},L_{\widetilde{X}})\\
 \to H^1(\widetilde{X},L_{\widetilde{X}}(M))
 \to H^1(M,L_{\widetilde{X}}(M)|_M)
 \to 0.
\end{multline*}
 
Taking the alternating sum of dimensions yields
 
\[
 h^1(L_{\widetilde{X}})
 -h^1(L_{\widetilde{X}}(M))
 =
 \chi(L_{\widetilde{X}}(M)|_M)-a_{\widetilde{X}}.
\]

Finally, the sequence
 
\[
 0 \to \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-M)
 \to \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}
 \to \mathcal{O}_M
 \to 0
\]
 
induces
 
\[
 0
 \to \mathbb{C}
 \to H^0(M,\mathcal{O}_M)
 \to H^1(\widetilde{X},\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-M))
 \to H^1(\widetilde{X},\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}})
 \to H^1(M,\mathcal{O}_M)
 \to 0,
\]
 
where the first term is \(A/\mathfrak{m}_A\). Consequently,
 
\[
 p_g-h^1(\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-M)) = 1-\chi(\mathcal{O}_M).
\]

Riemann--Roch applies to the effective Cartier cycle \(M\), without any reducedness assumption. For an invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{L}\) on \(\widetilde{X}\), it gives
 
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \chi(\mathcal{O}_M)
 &=-\frac12 M\cdot(M+K_{\widetilde{X}}),\\
 \chi(\mathcal{L}|_M)-\chi(\mathcal{O}_M)
 &=c_1(\mathcal{L})\cdot M.
 \end{aligned}
\]
 
Applying the second formula to
 
\[
 \mathcal{L}=L_{\widetilde{X}}(M)
 =\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}
   (M-K_{\widetilde{X}}-\widetilde{E}),
\]
 
and combining the three cohomology identities, we obtain
\begin{align}\label{eq:cycleindex}
 \Delta_{\widetilde{X}}+a_{\widetilde{X}}
 &=
 j_f-1+(p_g-h^1(\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}(-M)))
 +h^1(L_{\widetilde{X}})
 -h^1(L_{\widetilde{X}}(M))
 +a_{\widetilde{X}}\notag\\
 &=
 j_f+\chi(L_{\widetilde{X}}(M)|_M)
 -\chi(\mathcal{O}_M)\notag\\
 &=
 j_f+M^2-(K_{\widetilde{X}}+\widetilde{E})\cdot M.
\end{align}

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:milnor-cycle} with \((Y,D,Z)=(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{E},M)\). Combining \eqref{eq:correction}, \eqref{eq:cycleindex}, and \eqref{eq:milnor}, we conclude that
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)=\Delta(A)
 =
 \Delta_{\widetilde{X}}+a_{\widetilde{X}}
 =
 j_f+\chi(F_f)
 =
 1+j_f-\mu_f.
 \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
The \emph{equivariant Wahl defect} of \((Y,F)\) is
 
\[
 \mathcal{D}_Y :=[H^1(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y)]-[H^1(Y,S)]+[H^1(Y,L)] \in R(G),
\]
 
where \(S=\Theta_Y(-\log F)\), \(L=\bigwedge^2 S\), and \(R(G)\) is the complex representation ring of \(G\). Here \([M]\) denotes the class of a finite-dimensional complex \(G\)-representation \(M\), and \(\mathbf{1}\) denotes the class of the one-dimensional trivial representation.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:log-comparison}
The inclusion
 
\[
 \Omega_Y^\bullet(\log F) \hookrightarrow \mathscr{C}_D^\bullet
\]
 
is a \(G\)-equivariant quasi-isomorphism. Consequently,
 
\[
 \mathbb{H}^k(Y,\mathscr{C}_D^\bullet) \simeq H^k(U,\mathbb{C}).
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
We first prove that the quotient complex is exact. At a node, choose coordinates with
 
\[
 F=(xy=0),\quad D=a(x=0)+b(y=0),\quad a,b \geq 0.
\]
 
Write forms in the basis \(d\log x,d\log y\). The quotient is represented by convergent Laurent series whose monomials \(x^iy^j\) satisfy
 
\[
 i \geq -a,\quad j \geq -b,\quad i<0\text{ or }j<0.
\]
 
On the exterior algebra multiplying such a monomial, the differential is exterior multiplication by \(i d\log x+j d\log y\). If \(i<0\), contraction with \(x\partial_x\), divided by \(i\), is a homotopy between the identity and zero. For the remaining monomials, \(i \geq 0\) and \(j<0\), use contraction with \(y\partial_y\), divided by \(j\). In both cases,
 
\[
 dh+hd=\mathrm{id}.
\]
 
The negative powers are bounded, and the divisors \(i,j\) used here are nonzero integers. The operations therefore preserve convergence after shrinking the coordinate polydisc.

At a smooth point of \(F\), use the same homotopy in the normal coordinate. The tangential differential anticommutes with the contraction, so the identity remains valid. Away from \(F\), the quotient is zero. This proves exactness of the quotient complex.

For completeness, the ordinary logarithmic complex computes \(Rj_*\mathbb{C}_U\), where \(j\colon U \hookrightarrow Y\). Locally at a point where \(k\) branches of \(F\) meet, the complement is a product of \(k\) punctured discs and \(2-k\) discs. Its de Rham cohomology is the exterior algebra generated by the classes of \(d\log x_1,\ldots,d\log x_k\). The logarithmic complex has the same local cohomology: nonconstant monomials are contracted as above, and the holomorphic Poincar\'{e} lemma applies in the remaining coordinates. This proves the local comparison, and hence the claimed hypercohomology identification. The inclusions commute with the \(G\)-action. Equivariance of the local homotopies is not needed for an equivariant quasi-isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:comparison}
The spaces \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{Q}\) are finite-dimensional \(G\)-representations, and
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comparison}
 [\mathbb{C}_\kappa]\mathcal{D}_Y=\mathbf{1}+[\mathcal{Q}]-[\mathcal{P}].
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
We compare the two rows of coherent cohomology with the cohomology of the link, whose contributions in degrees one and two cancel. The hypercohomology spectral sequence is
 
\[
 E_1^{p,q}=H^q(Y,\mathscr{C}_D^p)
 \Rightarrow H^{p+q}(U,\mathbb{C}).
\]
 
By \eqref{eq:coherent-vanishing}, only the rows \(q=0,1\) can be nonzero. Let
 
\[
 W^\bullet=[H^1(Y,\mathscr{C}_D^0) \xrightarrow{d}
 H^1(Y,\mathscr{C}_D^1) \xrightarrow{d}
 H^1(Y,\mathscr{C}_D^2)],
\]
 
and put \(K=H^0(W^\bullet)\), \(M=H^1(W^\bullet)\), and \(N=H^2(W^\bullet)\). These three spaces are finite dimensional. The \(E_2\)-page has the following two rows:
 
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
q=1&K&M&N\\
q=0&\mathbb{C}&\mathcal{P}&\mathcal{Q}\\ \hline
 &p=0&p=1&p=2.
\end{array}
\]
 
The only potentially nonzero differential after \(E_1\) is
 
\[
 d_2^{0,1}\colon K \to \mathcal{Q}.
\]
 
In particular, \(N\) survives to \(E_\infty\). It is the only term of total degree three, and therefore
 
\[
 N \simeq H^3(U,\mathbb{C}).
\]
 
The punctured surface retracts onto its connected, oriented link. Holomorphic automorphisms preserve the orientation. Hence
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:orientation}
 N \simeq \mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{1}}.
\end{equation}

The filtrations on total cohomology in degrees one and two give the exact sequence
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:edge}
\begin{split}
0 \to \mathcal{P} \to H^1(U,\mathbb{C}) \to K
 \xrightarrow{d_2} \mathcal{Q} \to H^2(U,\mathbb{C}) \to M \to 0.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
 
For example, the quotient of \(H^1(U,\mathbb{C})\) by \(\mathcal{P}\) is \(\ker d_2\), while the kernel of \(H^2(U,\mathbb{C}) \to M\) is \(\operatorname{coker} d_2\). This also proves that \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{Q}\) are finite dimensional.

Poincar\'{e} duality on the link is equivariant and gives
 
\[
 H^2(U,\mathbb{C}) \simeq H^1(U,\mathbb{C})^*.
\]
 
The representation \(H^1(U,\mathbb{C})\) is the complexification of a real representation. Averaging a positive definite real inner product over \(G\) and complexifying gives an equivariant isomorphism with its dual. Thus
 
\begin{equation*}                      
 [H^1(U,\mathbb{C})]=[H^2(U,\mathbb{C})]\quad\text{in }R(G).
\end{equation*}
 
Taking the alternating sum in \eqref{eq:edge} now yields
 
\[
 [K]-[M]=[\mathcal{Q}]-[\mathcal{P}].
\]
 
Together with \eqref{eq:orientation}, this gives
 
\[
 \chi_G(W^\bullet)=\mathbf{1}+[\mathcal{Q}]-[\mathcal{P}].
\]
 
On the other hand, \eqref{eq:twists} identifies the three terms of \(W^\bullet\) with \(\mathbb{C}_\kappa\) tensored with
 
\[
 H^1(Y,L),\quad H^1(Y,S),\quad H^1(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y),
\]
 
in that order. Their alternating sum is \([\mathbb{C}_\kappa]\mathcal{D}_Y\), proving \eqref{eq:comparison}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Equation~\eqref{eq:comparison} is an identity in \(R(G)\). Its proof does not imply that \([\mathcal{Q}]-[\mathcal{P}]\) is effective. The residue argument in the next subsection establishes this additional assertion without choosing an injection \(\mathcal{P} \to \mathcal{Q}\).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:closed-one-forms}
Restriction induces a \(G\)-equivariant injection
 
\[
 \iota\colon\mathcal{P} \hookrightarrow \bigoplus_iH^0(F_i,\omega_{F_i}) \hookrightarrow W_F.
\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
A class in \(\mathcal{P}\) is represented by a closed holomorphic one-form \(\alpha\) on the punctured surface. By the extension theorem for closed one-forms, \(\alpha\) extends to a holomorphic one-form \(\widetilde{\alpha}\) on \(Y\); see Jörder~\cite[Proposition~1.2]{JorderExtension}. The extension is unique and remains closed, since its exterior derivative vanishes on the dense open set \(U\). Restricting to the components of \(F\) therefore defines an element of \(\bigoplus_iH^0(F_i,\omega_{F_i})\).

If \(\alpha=df\) for \(f \in B\), the pullback of \(f\) is constant on \(F\), and \(df\) restricts to zero on every \(F_i\). Thus restriction is well defined on \(\mathcal{P}\).

Suppose that the restriction of \(\widetilde{\alpha}\) to every component is zero. Every one-cycle on \(F\) is represented by a finite sum of piecewise smooth loops whose arcs lie on its components. The integral of \(\widetilde{\alpha}\) along each arc is zero. Thus all periods on \(F\) vanish, including periods corresponding to cycles in the dual graph. A sufficiently small resolution neighborhood retracts onto \(F\), so all periods on \(Y\) vanish as well. Integrating \(\widetilde{\alpha}\) from a fixed point gives a single-valued holomorphic function \(f\) on \(Y\) with \(df=\widetilde{\alpha}\). Since \(H^0(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y)=B\), this function comes from \(B\). The original class is therefore zero in \(\mathcal{P}\).

Uniqueness of extension and naturality of restriction show that \(\iota\) is equivariant.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:exact-residue}
Let \((Y,F)\) be a good resolution of a normal complex surface singularity, and put \(U=Y\setminus F\). If \(\beta \in H^0(Y,\omega_Y(F))\) satisfies \(\beta=d\alpha\) on \(U\) for some \(\alpha \in H^0(U,\Omega_U^1)\), then \(\operatorname{Res}(\beta)=0\).
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Fix a component \(F_i\), and let \(\gamma\) be a smooth closed loop in \(F_i\) avoiding the nodes. The normal circle bundle of small radius over \(\gamma\) is a closed oriented torus \(T_{\gamma,\epsilon} \subset U\). Orient it so that integration along the normal circle gives the usual factor \(2\pi i\). The residue integral formula gives
 
\[
 2\pi i\int_\gamma\operatorname{Res}_{F_i}(\beta)
 =\lim_{\epsilon \to 0}\int_{T_{\gamma,\epsilon}}\beta.
\]
 
For each sufficiently small \(\epsilon\), Stokes' theorem on this closed torus gives
 
\[
 \int_{T_{\gamma,\epsilon}}\beta
 =\int_{T_{\gamma,\epsilon}}d\alpha=0.
\]
 
Thus every period of \(\operatorname{Res}_{F_i}(\beta)\) away from the nodes is zero.

The differential \(\operatorname{Res}_{F_i}(\beta)\) has at most simple poles at the nodes. Applying the preceding calculation to small loops around the nodes shows that the residues of all these poles vanish. The poles are therefore removable. We obtain a holomorphic differential on the compact smooth curve \(F_i\) with all periods zero. It has a single-valued holomorphic primitive, which is constant by compactness. Hence \(\operatorname{Res}_{F_i}(\beta)=0\). This holds for every component, and proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:residue-sequence}
Residue induces an exact sequence of \(G\)-representations
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residue-sequence}
 0 \to I_{\mathrm{reg}} \to I_{\log} \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Res}} W_F \to 0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Two logarithmic two-forms represent the same class in \(\mathcal{Q}\) precisely when their difference is \(d\alpha\) for a holomorphic one-form \(\alpha\) on \(U\). Lemma~\ref{lem:exact-residue} shows that they have the same residue. Thus residue is well defined on \(I_{\log}\).

By \eqref{eq:adjunction}, a logarithmic two-form has zero residue if and only if it is regular on \(Y\). Hence the kernel of the induced map on \(I_{\log}\) is exactly \(I_{\mathrm{reg}}\). Finally, \eqref{eq:GR} and the cohomology sequence of \eqref{eq:adjunction} show that
 
\[
 H^0(Y,\omega_Y(F)) \to H^0(F,\omega_F)
\]
 
is surjective. The induced map from \(I_{\log}\) is therefore surjective. All maps commute with \(G\), and all spaces are finite dimensional by Proposition~\ref{prop:comparison} and compactness of \(F\).
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:effective}
With the notation above, put
 
\[
 \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}} := I_{\mathrm{reg}}\oplus(W_F/\mathcal{P})\oplus(\mathcal{Q}/I_{\log}).
\]
 
Then \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}}\) is a finite-dimensional \(G\)-representation and
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:effective}
 [\mathbb{C}_\kappa]\mathcal{D}_Y=\mathbf{1}+[\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}}].
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-one-forms} defines the quotient \(W_F/\mathcal{P}\). Proposition~\ref{prop:residue-sequence} gives
 
\[
 [\mathcal{Q}]=[I_{\mathrm{reg}}]+[W_F]+[\mathcal{Q}/I_{\log}].
\]
 
Subtracting \([\mathcal{P}]\) and applying Proposition~\ref{prop:comparison} proves \eqref{eq:effective}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:complex}
The representation in Theorem~\ref{thm:effective} is the cohomology of a naturally defined finite-dimensional complex. Put
 
\[
 \mathscr{K}^{-1}=\mathcal{P},\quad
 \mathscr{K}^0=I_{\mathrm{reg}}\oplus W_F\oplus(\mathcal{Q}/I_{\log}),
\]
 
with differential \(p \mapsto (0,\iota(p),0)\). Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-one-forms} gives
 
\[
 H^{-1}(\mathscr{K}^\bullet)=0,\quad
 H^0(\mathscr{K}^\bullet)=\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}}.
\]
 
No splitting of \eqref{eq:residue-sequence} is used in this construction.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:der-descent}
Restriction gives an isomorphism
 
\[
 (\operatorname{Der}_\mathbb{C} B)^G \simeq \operatorname{Der}_\mathbb{C} A.
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
An invariant derivation of \(B\) preserves \(A\). Conversely, a derivation of \(A\) lifts uniquely over the finite \'{e}tale map of punctured surfaces. For each \(b \in B\), its derivative under this lifted vector field is holomorphic on the punctured normal surface and extends across the singular point by Hartogs' theorem. These extensions define a derivation of \(B\), since the Leibniz identity holds on the punctured surface and hence everywhere. Uniqueness of the lift makes it invariant. The two constructions are inverse to one another.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:invariant-function}
Put \(n=|G|\). There is a function \(f \in \mathfrak{m}_A\) such that
 
\begin{equation*}                            
 \operatorname{div}_Y(f)=M+H,\quad M=\sum_i m_iF_i,\quad
 m_i>0,\quad n \mid m_i,
\end{equation*}
 
where \(H\) is reduced, smooth, transverse to \(F\), and disjoint from its nodes. On both \(A\) and \(B\), the function defines a reduced curve and has an isolated critical point. Its Milnor fibers are connected.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Choose an effective invariant exceptional cycle \(C\) with \(C\cdot F_i<0\) for every component, and such that every coefficient of \(C\) is divisible by \(n\). Such a cycle is obtained from a strictly anti-nef integral cycle by summing its translates and multiplying by \(n\). The invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{O}_Y(-C)\) is relatively ample over the contraction.

The stabilizer of every point acts trivially on the fiber of \(\mathcal{O}_Y(-C)\): this sheaf is the \(n\)-th power of an invariant divisorial sheaf, and stabilizer characters have orders dividing \(n\). It therefore descends to an invertible sheaf on \(Y/G\). A sufficiently high power is relatively generated and separates first jets along the quotient exceptional curves. Pulling back a general section gives an invariant function \(f \in \mathfrak{m}_A\) with exceptional part \(M\), a positive multiple of \(C\). To see transversality, choose the section to have simple zeros on the quotient curves away from points with larger stabilizers. The generic pointwise stabilizer fixes the tangential coordinate, so these simple tangential zeros remain simple after pullback. A general section also avoids the finitely many excluded points.

After shrinking, the function has no critical point away from the singular point on either surface. This can also be checked from the local expressions in Lemma~\ref{lem:logarithmic-differential} and the fact that the quotient map is \'{e}tale away from the singular point. The curve sections are generically reduced Cartier sections of Cohen--Macaulay surfaces, so they are reduced. Their Milnor fibers are connected: in the Milnor fibration of the link complement, a meridian around a reduced branch maps with degree one to the circle. The induced homomorphism to \(\mathbb{Z}\) is therefore surjective, and the fiber has one connected component.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:df}
For \(f\) as in Lemma~\ref{lem:invariant-function}, there is an equivariant exact sequence
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:df-sequence}
 0 \to L(M) \to S \xrightarrow{df} \mathcal{O}_Y(-M) \to 0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The local calculation in Lemma~\ref{lem:logarithmic-differential} gives the exact sequence after shrinking. Taking determinants identifies the kernel with \(\det S\otimes\mathcal{O}_Y(M)=L(M)\). This identification and the map \(df\) are equivariant because \(f\) is invariant.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:critical}
In \(R(G)\), one has
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical}
 [B/J]=\mathcal{D}_Y+\mathcal{T}_M.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The cohomology sequence of \(\mathcal{O}_Y(-M) \subset \mathcal{O}_Y\) gives
 
\[
 [H^1(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y)]-[H^1(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y(-M))]
 =[B/H^0(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y(-M))]-\chi_G(\mathcal{O}_M).
\]
 
The image of \(H^0(Y,S) \to H^0(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y(-M))\) is the critical ideal \(J=df(\operatorname{Der}_\mathbb{C} B)\), by \eqref{eq:der-lifting}. Thus \eqref{eq:df-sequence} gives
 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 [H^1(Y,S)]
 &=[H^1(Y,L(M))]+[H^1(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y(-M))]\\
 &\quad-[B/J]+[B/H^0(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y(-M))].
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
 
Finally, \eqref{eq:twists} and \eqref{eq:Hartogs} give
 
\[
 H^0(Y,L)=H^0(Y,L(M))=B\otimes\mathbb{C}_{\kappa^{-1}}.
\]
 
The sequence of \(L \subset L(M)\) therefore implies
 
\[
 [H^1(Y,L)]-[H^1(Y,L(M))]=\chi_G(L(M)|_M).
\]
 
Combining these three identities proves \eqref{eq:critical}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-trace}
Let a finite group \(G\) of order \(n\) act on a smooth surface \(Y\), preserving a compact simple normal crossing divisor \(F=\sum_iF_i\), and freely on \(Y\setminus F\). Let \(M=\sum_i m_iF_i\) be a \(G\)-invariant divisor with \(m_i>0\) and \(n \mid m_i\). Write \(L=\bigwedge^2\Theta_Y(-\log F)\), and give \(L(M)=L\otimes\mathcal{O}_Y(M)\) its natural linearization. Fix \(g \in G\), \(g \neq 1\).
\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(g\) preserves \(F_i\), then
 
\[
 \chi_g(\mathcal{O}_{m_iF_i})=\chi_g(L(M)|_{m_iF_i}).
\]
 
\item If \(g\) fixes a node \(p \in F_i\cap F_j\), put
 
\[
 N_p=\mathcal{O}_{Y,p}/(x^{m_i},y^{m_j}),
\]
 
where \(F_i=(x=0)\) and \(F_j=(y=0)\). Give \(N_p\) the action induced by local functions, with an additional minus sign when \(g\) exchanges the branches. Then
 
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(g \mid N_p)=\operatorname{tr}(g \mid L(M)\otimes N_p).
\]
 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Since \(M\) is \(n\) times an invariant integral divisor, \(\mathcal{O}_Y(M)\) has trivial stabilizer action on every fiber. We use eigenvalues for the induced action on local functions and their differentials. In particular, the conormal eigenvalue along \(C=(x=0)\) is the eigenvalue on the class of \(x\) in \(\mathcal{O}_Y(-C)|_C\).

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 1: \(g\) preserves \(C=F_i\) and acts nontrivially on it.} Put \(m=m_i\). The filtration of \(\mathcal{O}_{mC}\) by powers of the ideal of \(C\) has quotients \(\mathcal{O}_C(-kC)\), \(0 \leq k<m\). At a fixed point \(p\) of \(g|_C\), let \(\mu \neq 1\) be the eigenvalue on the cotangent line of \(C\), \(\lambda\) the conormal eigenvalue, and \(\tau\) the character on the fiber of \(L(M)\). The holomorphic Lefschetz formula on \(C\)~\cite{AtiyahBott1967} gives the difference of local contributions
 
\[
 \frac{1-\tau}{1-\mu}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\lambda^k.
\]
 
At a smooth point of \(F\), one has \(\lambda \neq 1\). Otherwise finite-order linearization would give a fixed transverse curve, contrary to freeness on \(Y\setminus F\). Since the order of \(\lambda\) divides \(n\) and \(n \mid m\), the sum is zero. At a node, both branches are preserved. The logarithmic vector fields \(x\partial_x,y\partial_y\) have trivial action on their fibers, so \(\tau=1\). Thus all local contributions vanish. If \(g|_C\) has no fixed point, the Lefschetz formula gives zero directly.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 2: \(g\) fixes \(C=F_i\) pointwise.} Its conormal character \(\lambda\) is constant and nontrivial. The action on the fiber of the logarithmic determinant, and hence of \(L(M)\), is trivial at a general point and therefore on all of \(C\). On the \(k\)-th quotient, Riemann--Roch gives
 
\[
 \chi_g(\mathcal{O}_C(-kC))-\chi_g(L(M)|_C\otimes\mathcal{O}_C(-kC))
 =-\lambda^k\deg(L(M)|_C).
\]
 
The conormal degrees cancel in this difference. Summing over \(0 \leq k<m_i\) gives zero because \(n \mid m_i\). This proves the first assertion.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 3: \(g\) fixes a node and preserves both branches.} The fiber character of the logarithmic determinant is one, as in Case 1, so the same holds for \(L(M)\). Averaging a local frame of \(L(M)\) over the cyclic group generated by \(g\) gives an invariant frame. Thus \(N_p\) and \(L(M)\otimes N_p\) are isomorphic as representations, and their traces agree.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 4: \(g\) fixes a node and exchanges the branches.} Invariance of \(M\) gives \(m_i=m_j=m\). On the cotangent space, write
 
\[
 x \mapsto \alpha y,\quad y \mapsto \beta x.
\]
 
The associated graded of \(\mathcal{O}_{Y,p}/(x^m,y^m)\) has basis \(x^ay^b\), \(0 \leq a,b<m\). Only the terms with \(a=b\) contribute to the trace of the action induced by local functions, which is
 
\[
 \sum_{a=0}^{m-1}(\alpha\beta)^a.
\]
 
Here \(\alpha\beta \neq 1\), since otherwise linearization would give a fixed curve transverse to both branches. The order of \(\alpha\beta\) divides \(n\), and \(n \mid m\), so this sum is zero. The additional sign in the action on \(N_p\) does not change the vanishing. On the logarithmic tangent fiber the two basis vectors are exchanged, so the fiber character of \(L(M)\) is \(-1\). A local eigenvector frame of \(L(M)\) identifies its tensor action with this scalar times the action on \(N_p\). Its trace is therefore also zero. This proves the second assertion.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:trace}
For every \(g \in G\) with \(g \neq 1\),
 
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(g \mid \mathcal{T}_M)=0.
\]
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The normalization sequence of the nonreduced cycle is
 
\[
 0 \to \mathcal{O}_M \to \bigoplus_i\mathcal{O}_{m_iF_i}
 \to \bigoplus_{p \in F_i\cap F_j}N_p \to 0.
\]
 
The last map is the difference of the branch restrictions. Consequently, an interchange of branches contributes the minus sign used in Lemma~\ref{lem:local-trace}. Tensor this sequence by \(L(M)\) and subtract equivariant Euler characteristics. Summands permuted without being fixed by \(g\) have zero trace. For the fixed summands, the two assertions of Lemma~\ref{lem:local-trace} give zero difference. Hence \(\operatorname{tr}(g \mid \mathcal{T}_M)=0\).
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:transfer}
Under the hypotheses of this subsection,
 
\[
 \Delta(A)=\operatorname{mult}_{\mathbf{1}}(\mathcal{D}_Y).
\]
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:der-descent} and exactness of invariants,
 
\[
 (B/df(\operatorname{Der}_\mathbb{C} B))^G
 \simeq A/df(\operatorname{Der}_\mathbb{C} A).
\]
 
The quotient \(F_f/G\) is the Milnor fiber of \(f\) on \(A\), and the finite covering gives
 
\[
 H^1(F_f/G,\mathbb{C}) \simeq H^1(F_f,\mathbb{C})^G.
\]
 
Taking trivial multiplicities in \eqref{eq:milnorrep} therefore yields
 
\[
 \operatorname{mult}_{\mathbf{1}}(\mathcal{D}_Y)=1+j_A(f)-\mu_A(f).
\]
 
Formula~\eqref{eq:function-index} identifies this with \(\Delta(A)\).
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:negative-log}
Let \(F\) be a simple normal crossing divisor on a smooth surface \(Y\), let \(T\) be an effective divisor with support \(F\) and strictly positive coefficients, and let \(j\colon Y\setminus F \hookrightarrow Y\). Then
 
\[
 \Omega_Y^\bullet(\log F)(-T) \simeq j_!\mathbb{C}_{Y\setminus F}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Away from \(F\), the assertion is the holomorphic Poincar\'{e} lemma. At a smooth point of \(F=(x=0)\), write coefficients in powers \(x^a\) with \(a \geq t>0\), using \(d\log x\) as the normal differential. On each such term, contraction with \(x\partial_x\), divided by \(a\), is a contracting homotopy. The tangential differential anticommutes with this contraction. At a node, the coefficients are sums of \(x^ay^b\) with \(a,b>0\), and the same contraction applies. Division by positive integers preserves convergence on smaller polydiscs. Thus the complex has zero stalk cohomology along \(F\). The natural map from \(j_!\mathbb{C}_{Y\setminus F}\) is consequently a quasi-isomorphism. The construction is equivariant whenever the divisor and the group action are equivariant.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:ADE-zero}
Suppose that \(B\) is a rational double point and \((Y,F)\) is its minimal resolution. Then \(\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{Q}=0\) and \(\mathcal{D}_Y=0\) in \(R(G)\). If \(B\) is smooth, the same assertions hold with \(Y\) the blowup of the origin and \(F\) its exceptional curve.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
\emph{The rational double point case.} Suppose that \(B\) is a rational double point. The resolution is crepant, so \(Z=0\) and \(D=-F\). The complex corresponding to \eqref{eq:polar-complex} is now
 
\[
 \mathscr{C}_{-F}^\bullet=
 [\mathcal{O}_Y(-F) \to \Omega_Y^1(\log F)(-F) \to \omega_Y].
\]
 
By Lemma~\ref{lem:negative-log}, it computes \(j_!\mathbb{C}_U\). A sufficiently small resolution neighborhood retracts onto \(F\). The exact sequence \(0 \to j_!\mathbb{C}_U \to \mathbb{C}_Y \to \mathbb{C}_F \to 0\) therefore gives
 
\[
 \mathbb{H}^k(Y,\mathscr{C}_{-F}^\bullet)=0\quad\text{for every }k.
\]

Write \(B=\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}^H\) with \(H \subset \operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})\) finite. Reflexive forms on \(B\) identify with \(H\)-invariant regular forms on \(\mathbb{C}^2\): pull back over the punctured surface and extend the coefficients across the origin. The radial homotopy for the holomorphic de Rham complex commutes with \(H\). It proves \(\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{Q}=0\).

The global-section complex of \(\mathscr{C}_{-F}^\bullet\) is
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ADE-global}
 [\mathfrak{m}_B \to \Omega_B^{[1]} \to \omega_B].
\end{equation}
 
For its first term, a function vanishes along \(F\) precisely when its value at the singular point is zero. The middle term follows from lifting of derivations and contraction with the nowhere vanishing canonical form; the last term follows from crepancy. The radial homotopy just described contracts \eqref{eq:ADE-global}, since constants have been removed from degree zero.

Only the rows \(q=0,1\) occur in the coherent hypercohomology spectral sequence. The first has zero cohomology, and total hypercohomology is zero. Thus the second row is acyclic. Its alternating class is \([\mathbb{C}_\kappa]\mathcal{D}_Y\), by the contraction identifications \eqref{eq:twists}, which remain valid for \(D=-F\). Hence \(\mathcal{D}_Y=0\).

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{The smooth case.} Suppose that \(B=\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}\) and \(Y\) is the blowup of the origin. The pullback of \(dx\wedge dy\) has divisor \(F\). Thus \(Z=-F\), \(D=-2F\), and the relevant complex is \(\Omega_Y^\bullet(\log F)(-2F)\). Its hypercohomology again vanishes by Lemma~\ref{lem:negative-log} and the retraction onto \(F\). Its global-section complex is
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:smooth-global}
 [\mathfrak{m}_B^2 \to \mathfrak{m}_B\Omega_B^1 \to \Omega_B^2].
\end{equation}
 
Indeed, \(H^0(\mathcal{O}_Y(-2F))=\mathfrak{m}_B^2\). Logarithmic vector fields descend to the vector fields vanishing at the origin, and all such vector fields lift to the blowup. Contraction with \(dx\wedge dy\) gives the middle term. Finally, \(\omega_Y(-F)\) is the pullback of \(\omega_B\).

On a homogeneous form of total radial weight \(w>0\), contraction with \(x\partial_x+y\partial_y\), divided by \(w\), gives the usual homotopy. On \eqref{eq:smooth-global}, it sends one-forms with coefficients in \(\mathfrak{m}_B\) to functions in \(\mathfrak{m}_B^2\), and two-forms to one-forms with coefficients in \(\mathfrak{m}_B\). The complex is therefore acyclic. The same spectral sequence argument gives \(\mathcal{D}_Y=0\). The ordinary Poincar\'{e} lemma gives \(\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{Q}=0\).
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:constant}
The quotient of the full reflexive de Rham complex by \eqref{eq:ADE-global} is \(\mathbb{C}[0]\). In the smooth case the quotient is
 
\[
 [B/\mathfrak{m}_B^2 \xrightarrow{d}
       \Omega_B^1/\mathfrak{m}_B\Omega_B^1],
\]
 
which is also quasi-isomorphic to \(\mathbb{C}[0]\): differentiation identifies the linear functions with the constant one-forms. Thus both cases remove the same trivial representation at the level of complexes. The term \(\mathbf{1}\) in \eqref{eq:effective-Hm} cannot be retained when the polar divisor is negative.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:invariant-plane-function}
There exists a reduced \(\Gamma\)-invariant homogeneous polynomial \(f(x,y)\) of degree \(n\).
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The degree-\(n\) invariant linear system on \(\mathbb{P}^1\) has no base point. At a prescribed point \([v]\), choose a linear form \(\ell\) that does not vanish at any point in its finite orbit. Then the invariant product \(\prod_{g \in \Gamma}g\ell\) does not vanish at \([v]\). The resulting base point free system defines a nonconstant morphism from \(\mathbb{P}^1\), because its line bundle has positive degree. In characteristic zero this morphism is generically unramified onto its image. A general hyperplane avoids the finitely many exceptional values and meets the image transversely. Its pullback has distinct zeros. The corresponding invariant homogeneous polynomial is reduced.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:plane-representations}
There are isomorphisms of \(\Gamma\)-representations
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:plane-representations}
 \begin{aligned}
 J_f& \simeq \mathbb{C}_{\chi^{-1}}\oplus\mathbb{C}[\Gamma]^{\oplus(n-2)},\\
 H^1(F_f,\mathbb{C})& \simeq \mathbb{C}\oplus\mathbb{C}[\Gamma]^{\oplus(n-2)}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
 
Consequently,
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:plane-index}
 \mathbf{1}+[J_f]-[H^1(F_f,\mathbb{C})]=[\mathbb{C}_{\chi^{-1}}]
 \quad\text{in }R(\Gamma).
\end{equation}
 
The isomorphisms in \eqref{eq:plane-representations} are not asserted to be canonical.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
\emph{The Jacobian representation.} Since \(f\) is reduced and homogeneous in two variables, its gradient vanishes only at the origin. For if a nonzero point were critical, Euler's identity would put it on \(f=0\), whose distinct lines meet only at the origin and are smooth elsewhere. Thus \(f_x,f_y\) form a regular sequence. The graded algebra \(J_f\) has dimension \((n-1)^2\), which is also the Milnor number of \(f\); see \cite{Milnor} for the Milnor fiber and Jacobian algebra comparison.

The two partial derivatives span a copy of \(V^*\): the map \(V^* \to \mathbb{C}[x,y]_{n-1}\) sending a constant vector field to its derivative of \(f\) is equivariant and injective. The equivariant Koszul resolution therefore gives
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Koszul-character}
 \sum_{a \geq 0}\operatorname{tr}(g \mid (J_f)_a)t^a
 =\frac{\det(1-t^{n-1}g \mid V^*)}{\det(1-tg \mid V)}.
\end{equation}
 
If \(g \ne 1\), neither eigenvalue of \(g\) on \(V\) is \(1\), since a nonzero fixed vector would contradict freeness away from the origin. Putting \(t=1\) in \eqref{eq:Koszul-character} gives
 
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(g \mid J_f)
 =\frac{\det(1-g \mid V^*)}{\det(1-g \mid V)}
 =\chi(g)^{-1}.
\]
 
At the identity, \(\dim J_f=(n-1)^2=1+n(n-2)\). These are exactly the characters of the first representation in \eqref{eq:plane-representations}. Equality of characters implies an isomorphism because finite-group representations over \(\mathbb{C}\) are semisimple.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{The Milnor fiber representation.} By Milnor~\cite{Milnor}, the Milnor fiber is connected and has the homotopy type of a bouquet of \((n-1)^2\) circles. The group \(\Gamma\) acts freely on it, since the origin does not belong to a nonzero fiber. Lift a finite cell decomposition of \(F_f/\Gamma\) to \(F_f\). Each chain group is a sum of regular representations, and hence
 
\[
 \mathbf{1}-[H^1(F_f,\mathbb{C})]
 =\chi(F_f/\Gamma)[\mathbb{C}[\Gamma]].
\]
 
The Euler characteristic of the quotient is
 
\[
 \chi(F_f/\Gamma)
 =\frac{1-(n-1)^2}{n}=-(n-2).
\]
 
This proves the second isomorphism and then \eqref{eq:plane-index}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:quotient-zero}
If \(A=R_0^\Gamma\) is non-Gorenstein, then \(\Delta(A)=0\).
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
For a finite quotient that is unramified away from the origin, the canonical character is the determinant character. In particular, \(A\) is Gorenstein if and only if \(\chi=1\). One direction follows by descending \(dx\wedge dy\). For the other, a generator of a trivial canonical module pulls back on the punctured plane to \(u dx\wedge dy\), where \(u\) and \(u^{-1}\) extend holomorphically across the origin by Hartogs' theorem. Evaluating invariance at the origin gives \(\chi=1\). Here \(A\) is non-Gorenstein, so \(\chi \ne 1\).

The derivation descent argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:der-descent} applies also to the smooth algebra \(R_0\) and gives
 
\[
 (\operatorname{Der}_\mathbb{C} R_0)^\Gamma \simeq \operatorname{Der}_\mathbb{C} A.
\]
 
As \(f\) is invariant, \(df\) is equivariant. Exactness of invariants gives
 
\[
 J_f^\Gamma \simeq A/df(\operatorname{Der}_\mathbb{C} A).
\]
 
The Milnor fiber on \(A\) is \(F_f/\Gamma\); transfer identifies its cohomology with the invariant cohomology of \(F_f\). The descended curve \(f=0\) is reduced, since \(A/(f)=(R_0/(f))^\Gamma\) is reduced. Thus it satisfies the hypotheses of the function-index formula.

Taking invariants in \eqref{eq:plane-representations} gives
 
\[
 j_A(f)=n-2,\quad \mu_A(f)=n-1.
\]
 
The singularity \(A\) is non-Gorenstein, so it is not a rational double point, and \eqref{eq:function-index} applies. Therefore
 
\[
 \Delta(A)=1+j_A(f)-\mu_A(f)=0.
\]
 
Equivalently, \eqref{eq:plane-index} identifies this integer with \(\dim(\mathbb{C}_{\chi^{-1}})^\Gamma\), which vanishes.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let \((V,0)\) be a normal \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein complex surface singularity. Put
 
\[
 \varepsilon(V,0)=
 \begin{cases}
 1&\text{if \((V,0)\) is Gorenstein},\\
 0&\text{if \((V,0)\) is non-Gorenstein}.
 \end{cases}
\]
 
If \((V,0)\) is not a rational double point, then
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0) \geq \varepsilon(V,0),
\]
 
with equality if and only if \((V,0)\) is quasi-homogeneous. For a rational double point, \(\Delta(V,0)=0\).
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:uniform}
The space \(\mathcal{E}_B\) is a finite-dimensional \(G\)-representation, independent of the principalization, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-defect}
 \Delta(A)=\dim(\mathcal{E}_B)_\kappa
          =\dim(\mathcal{E}_B\otimes\mathbb{C}_{\kappa^{-1}})^G.
\end{equation}
If \(B\) is singular and not a rational double point, then \(T_B \simeq \mathbb{C}\) with trivial action, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-nonADE}
 \Delta(A)=\delta_{\kappa,1}+\dim(\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}})_\kappa.
\end{equation}
If \(B\) is smooth or a rational double point, then \(\mathcal{E}_B=0\) and \(\Delta(A)=0\).
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Suppose first that \(B\) is singular and not a rational double point. On its minimal good resolution, the canonical generator has a pole along every exceptional component. A regular two-form \(a\eta\) cannot have \(a\) a unit, since its pullback would then have the same poles. Consequently \(R_B \subset \mathfrak{m}_B\omega_B\), and
 
\[
 \omega_B/(R_B+\mathfrak{m}_B\omega_B)
 =\omega_B/\mathfrak{m}_B\omega_B \simeq \mathbb{C}_\kappa.
\]
 
This proves \(T_B \simeq \mathbb{C}\). Equation~\eqref{eq:effective-Hm} gives
 
\[
 [\mathbb{C}_\kappa]\mathcal{D}_Y=[\mathcal{E}_B].
\]
 
If \(G\) is trivial, the definition of the defect gives \(\Delta(A)=\dim\mathcal{D}_Y=1+\dim\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}}\). If \(G\) is nontrivial, Proposition~\ref{prop:transfer} gives \(\Delta(A)=\operatorname{mult}_{\mathbf{1}}(\mathcal{D}_Y)\). Taking character multiplicities proves \eqref{eq:uniform-defect} and \eqref{eq:uniform-nonADE}.

If \(B\) is smooth or a rational double point, then \(R_B=\omega_B\), so \(T_B=0\). Proposition~\ref{prop:ADE-zero} gives \(\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{Q}=0\) and hence \(\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}}=0\). If \(G\) is trivial and \(A\) is singular, then \(A=B\) is a rational double point, and the same proposition gives \(\Delta(A)=0\). If \(G\) is nontrivial, Section~\ref{sec:quotient-covers} gives \(\Delta(A)=0\) from the determinant character calculation and the function-index formula. Thus \eqref{eq:uniform-defect} holds in these cases as well.

All summands in \eqref{eq:uniform-representation} are finite-dimensional \(G\)-representations. Independence follows from the invariance of \(R_B\) and the principalization comparison in Section~\ref{subsec:maximal-ideal}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:graded-canonical-cover}
Let \((V,0)\) be a quasi-homogeneous normal complex \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein surface singularity of index \(r\), and let \(q\colon(\widetilde{V},0)\to(V,0)\) be its canonical cover, with covering group \(G\). Then \((\widetilde{V},0)\) admits a good \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action commuting with \(G\). The induced action on \((V,0)\) is the given action composed with \(t\mapsto t^r\).
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Put \(A:=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}\) and \(B:=\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{V},0}\). Choose a finitely generated positively graded normal \(\mathbb{C}\)-algebra \(R_0\), with \((R_0)_0=\mathbb{C}\), such that
 
\[
 A\simeq\mathcal{O}_{(\operatorname{Spec} R_0)^{\mathrm{an}},0}.
\]
 
The freeness of \(\omega_A^{[r]}\), faithful flatness of the local map from \(R_0\) to \(A\), and graded Nakayama's lemma give a homogeneous generator \(\theta\) of \(\omega_{R_0}^{[r]}\). Put \(d:=\deg\theta\).

Define the canonical cover
 
\[
 S:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r-1}\omega_{R_0}^{[i]},
\]
 
with multiplication determined by \(\theta\mapsto 1\). For a homogeneous element \(s\in(\omega_{R_0}^{[i]})_n\), put
 
\[
 \operatorname{wt}(s):=rn-id.
\]
 
By Singh~\cite[Proposition~4.2]{Singh2003}, these weights are nonnegative and the weight-zero part of \(S\) is \(\mathbb{C}\). For \(t\in\mathbb{C}^*\) and \(g\in G=\mu_r\), the formulas
 
\[
 t\cdot s:=t^{rn-id}s,\quad g\cdot s:=g^is
\]
 
define commuting actions on \(S\). The induced action on \(R_0\) multiplies an element of degree \(n\) by \(t^{rn}\), so it is the original action composed with \(t\mapsto t^r\).

The algebraic action on \(\operatorname{Spec} S\) defines a holomorphic action on \((\operatorname{Spec} S)^{\mathrm{an}}\). Its local ring at the vertex is
 
\[
 \mathcal{O}_{(\operatorname{Spec} S)^{\mathrm{an}},0}
 \simeq S\otimes_{R_0}A
 \simeq\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r-1}\omega_A^{[i]},
\]
 
with multiplication determined by the image of \(\theta\). The generator used to define \(B\) has the form \(u\theta\), where \(u\in A^\times\). Choose \(v\in A^\times\) with \(v^r=u\). Multiplication by \(v^i\) on the \(i\)th summand gives a \(G\)-equivariant \(A\)-algebra isomorphism from this local ring to \(B\). Through this isomorphism, the good \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action induces the required action on \((\widetilde{V},0)\).
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:analytic-weight-homotopy}
Let \(V_0^\bullet\) denote the weight-zero subcomplex of \(V^\bullet\) for the \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action. Then the inclusion \(V_0^\bullet\to V^\bullet\) is a \(G\)-equivariant chain homotopy equivalence.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Let \(\rho_\theta\) denote pullback by \(e^{i\theta}\). Choose an \(S^1\times G\)-invariant analytic representative. After shrinking, the pullbacks are defined for \(\theta\) in a complex neighborhood of \([0,2\pi]\). Define
 
\[
 \Pi_0\alpha:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\rho_\theta\alpha d\theta,\quad
 T\alpha:=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}(\theta-\pi)\rho_\theta\alpha d\theta.
\]
 
These integrals define analytic sections by Jörder~\cite[Proposition~4.10]{JorderPoincare2014}. They preserve holomorphicity on \(U\), so the resulting differential forms are reflexive. The resulting functions extend across \(0\) by normality. Both operators commute with \(d\); see Jörder~\cite[Remark~4.18]{JorderPoincare2014}. The operator \(\Pi_0\) is the projection onto \(V_0^\bullet\), since \(S^1\)-invariance is equivalent to weight zero for the \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action.

The identity \(\partial_\theta\rho_\theta=i\mathcal{L}_\xi\rho_\theta\) holds. The periodic averaging formula of Avenda\~{n}o Camacho and Vorobiev~\cite[Proposition~2.1]{AvendanoCamachoVorobiev2011} therefore gives
 
\[
 \mathcal{L}_\xi T=\mathrm{id}-\Pi_0.
\]
 
Put \(h:=\iota_\xi T\). Since \(T\) commutes with \(d\), Cartan's formula gives
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weight-homotopy}
 dh+hd=(d\iota_\xi+\iota_\xi d)T=\mathrm{id}-\Pi_0.
\end{equation}

The action of \(G\) commutes with the \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action. Hence \(\rho_\theta\), \(\Pi_0\), \(T\), and \(\iota_\xi\) commute with \(G\). Since \(\Pi_0\) restricts to the identity on \(V_0^\bullet\), equation~\eqref{eq:weight-homotopy} shows that \(\Pi_0\colon V^\bullet\to V_0^\bullet\) is a \(G\)-equivariant homotopy inverse of the inclusion.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:zero-weight-one-forms}
Every \(\alpha\in(\Omega_B^{[1]})_0\) satisfies
 
\[
 d\alpha=0,\quad \iota_\xi\alpha=0.
\]
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The function \(\iota_\xi\alpha\) has weight zero, so it is constant because \(B_0=\mathbb{C}\). Since \(\mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha=0\), Cartan's formula gives
 
\[
 \iota_\xi(d\alpha)
 =\mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha-d(\iota_\xi\alpha)=0.
\]
 
Choose an embedding of the positively graded algebraic model using homogeneous generators \(x_j\) of positive weights \(w_j\). Away from the origin, some \(x_j\) is nonzero, and the corresponding component \(w_jx_j\) of \(\xi\) is nonzero. Thus \(\xi\) is nowhere zero on \(U\). Since \(U\) is a smooth surface, contraction by \(\xi\) is injective on two-forms. Hence \(d\alpha=0\).

Suppose first that \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is singular. Using the positively graded algebraic model, choose a \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-equivariant resolution \(p\colon(Y,F)\to(\widetilde{V},0)\) with an algebraic action on \(F\). By van Straten--Steenbrink~\cite[Corollary~(1.4)]{VanStratenSteenbrink1985}, the closed one-form \(\alpha\) extends to a holomorphic one-form \(\widetilde{\alpha}\) on a neighborhood of \(F\); see also J\"{o}rder~\cite[Proposition~1.2]{JorderExtension}.

The proper algebraic fiber \(F\) has a \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-fixed point \(y\). Indeed, properness extends the algebraic orbit map \(t\mapsto t\cdot z\), for any \(z\in F\), to \(t=0\), and its limit is fixed. Let \(\widetilde{\xi}\) denote the lifted Euler vector field. Then \(\widetilde{\xi}(y)=0\). The identity
 
\[
 \widetilde{\alpha}(\widetilde{\xi})
 =p^*(\iota_\xi\alpha)
\]
 
holds on \(Y\setminus F\) and hence on a neighborhood of \(F\). Evaluating at \(y\) shows that the constant \(\iota_\xi\alpha\) is zero.

If \(\widetilde{V}\) is smooth at \(0\), then \(\alpha\) is holomorphic at \(0\). Evaluating there gives the same conclusion, since \(\xi(0)=0\).
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:Euler-PQ}
There is a \(G\)-equivariant isomorphism
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Euler-PQ}
 \mathcal{Q}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal{P},
 \quad [\beta]\longmapsto[\iota_\xi\Pi_0\beta],
\end{equation}
 
where \(\Pi_0\) is the projection onto the weight-zero part for the \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Since \(\xi\) is nowhere zero on the smooth surface \(U\), contraction induces a sheaf isomorphism
 
\[
 \iota_\xi\colon\Omega_U^2\xrightarrow{\sim}
 \ker(\iota_\xi\colon\Omega_U^1\to\mathcal{O}_U).
\]
 
Indeed, in local coordinates with \(\xi=\partial/\partial z_1\), contraction sends \(dz_1\wedge dz_2\) to \(dz_2\). Its inverse preserves the weights and commutes with \(G\), since it is unique and \(\xi\) is invariant under both actions. Lemma~\ref{lem:zero-weight-one-forms} therefore gives a \(G\)-equivariant isomorphism
 
\[
 \iota_\xi\colon(\omega_B)_0\xrightarrow{\sim}(\Omega_B^{[1]})_0.
\]

Both differentials in \(V_0^\bullet\) vanish: functions of weight zero are constant, and one-forms of weight zero are closed by Lemma~\ref{lem:zero-weight-one-forms}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:analytic-weight-homotopy}, the projection \(\Pi_0\) therefore induces canonical \(G\)-equivariant isomorphisms
 
\[
 \mathcal{Q}\simeq(\omega_B)_0,\quad
 \mathcal{P}\simeq(\Omega_B^{[1]})_0.
\]
 
Combining these isomorphisms with contraction gives \eqref{eq:Euler-PQ}. In particular, for every \(\alpha\in\Omega_B^{[1]}\),
 
\[
 \Pi_0(d\alpha)=d(\Pi_0\alpha)=0,
\]
 
so the displayed map is independent of the two-form representative.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:qh-residue-zero}
Let \((\widetilde{V},0)\) be a quasi-homogeneous Gorenstein normal complex surface singularity. We also allow \(\widetilde{V}\) to be smooth at \(0\). Put \(B:=\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{V},0}\). Then the residue representation \(\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}}\) vanishes. If \(\widetilde{V}\) is singular at \(0\) and \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is not a rational double point, then
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qh-residue-terms}
 I_{\mathrm{reg}}=0,\quad
 \mathcal{P}\xrightarrow[\iota]{\sim}W_F,\quad
 \mathcal{Q}=I_{\log}\xrightarrow[\operatorname{Res}]{\sim}W_F.
\end{equation}
 
Here \(\iota\) is the restriction map of Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-one-forms}, and \(\operatorname{Res}\) is the residue map in \eqref{eq:residue-sequence}.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
If \(\widetilde{V}\) is smooth at \(0\) or \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is a rational double point, Proposition~\ref{prop:ADE-zero} gives \(\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{Q}=0\). The definition \eqref{eq:Hm} therefore gives \(\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}}=0\).

Suppose now that \(\widetilde{V}\) is singular at \(0\) and \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is not a rational double point. Proposition~\ref{prop:Euler-PQ}, applied with the trivial group, gives \(\dim\mathcal{Q}=\dim\mathcal{P}\). This numerical equality also follows from Du--Yau~\cite[Proposition~3.3]{DuYau2010} and Wahl~\cite[Corollary~1.11]{Wahl1985}. Taking dimensions in \eqref{eq:Hm-class} gives
 
\[
 \dim\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}}
 =\dim\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}}
 =\dim\mathcal{Q}-\dim\mathcal{P}=0.
\]
 
Hence \(\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}}=0\).

Each summand in the direct sum defining \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}}\) in Theorem~\ref{thm:effective} must also vanish. Thus
 
\[
 I_{\mathrm{reg}}=0,\quad
 W_F/\mathcal{P}=0,\quad
 \mathcal{Q}/I_{\log}=0.
\]
 
The restriction map of Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-one-forms} is therefore an isomorphism. Since \(I_{\mathrm{reg}}=0\) and \(I_{\log}=\mathcal{Q}\), the residue exact sequence \eqref{eq:residue-sequence} gives the second isomorphism in \eqref{eq:qh-residue-terms}. Both maps are \(G\)-equivariant by their construction.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:qh-equality}
Let \((V,0)\) be a quasi-homogeneous normal \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein surface singularity, and put \(A=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}\). If \(A\) is Gorenstein and is not a rational double point, then \(\Delta(A)=1\). If \(A\) is non-Gorenstein, then \(\Delta(A)=0\). A rational double point has \(\Delta(A)=0\).
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Let \(q\colon(\widetilde{V},0)\to(V,0)\) be the canonical cover, with covering group \(G\), and put \(A:=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}\) and \(B:=\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{V},0}\). By Lemma~\ref{lem:graded-canonical-cover}, \((\widetilde{V},0)\) admits a good \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action commuting with \(G\). Corollary~\ref{cor:qh-residue-zero} gives \(\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}}=0\).

Suppose first that \((V,0)\) is Gorenstein and is not a rational double point. The canonical cover is trivial, so \(B=A\) and \(\kappa=1\). Equation~\eqref{eq:uniform-nonADE} therefore gives
 
\[
 \Delta(A)=\delta_{\kappa,1}=1.
\]

Suppose next that \((V,0)\) is non-Gorenstein. Then \(\kappa\ne 1\). If \(\widetilde{V}\) is singular at \(0\) and \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is not a rational double point, equation~\eqref{eq:uniform-nonADE} gives
 
\[
 \Delta(A)=\delta_{\kappa,1}=0.
\]
 
If the canonical cover is smooth or a rational double point, equation~\eqref{eq:exceptional-index} and the function-index formula \eqref{eq:function-index} give
 
\[
 \Delta(A)=\dim((\mathbb{C}_{\kappa^{-1}})^G)=0,
\]
 
since \(\kappa\) is nontrivial.

Finally, if \((V,0)\) is a rational double point, its canonical cover is trivial, and Proposition~\ref{prop:ADE-zero} gives \(\Delta(A)=0\).
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:unit-divergence}
If \(\operatorname{div}_\eta\delta\notin\mathfrak{m}_B\) for some \(\delta\in\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B)\), then \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is quasi-homogeneous.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Every derivation of \(B\) preserves \(\mathfrak{m}_B\), since its local flow preserves the isolated singular point. Suppose that \(\delta\) induces a nilpotent endomorphism of \(\mathfrak{m}_B/\mathfrak{m}_B^2\). Put \(a:=\operatorname{div}_\eta\delta\). We show that \(a(0)=0\).

Define
 
\[
 J_{\mathrm{can}}:=\{f\in B:f\eta\in\operatorname{im}(\Omega_B^2\to\omega_B)\}.
\]
 
This ideal is nonzero and is the unit ideal away from the singular point. Hence it is either \(B\) or \(\mathfrak{m}_B\)-primary. Lie differentiation preserves the image of K\"{a}hler two-forms, and
 
\[
 \mathcal{L}_\delta(f\eta)=(\delta(f)+af)\eta.
\]
 
Since \(aJ_{\mathrm{can}}\subseteq J_{\mathrm{can}}\), it follows that \(\delta(J_{\mathrm{can}})\subseteq J_{\mathrm{can}}\).

The action of \(\delta\) on coefficients and Lie differentiation of forms induce endomorphisms \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) of \(J_{\mathrm{can}}/\mathfrak{m}_BJ_{\mathrm{can}}\), respectively. For the latter, we use multiplication by \(\eta\) to identify the quotient with \((J_{\mathrm{can}}\eta)/\mathfrak{m}_B(J_{\mathrm{can}}\eta)\). Thus
 
\[
 T_1([f]):=[\delta(f)],\quad
 T_2([f]):=[\delta(f)+af],\quad
 T_2-T_1=a(0)\operatorname{id}.
\]

The induced derivation on each \(\mathfrak{m}_B^j/\mathfrak{m}_B^{j+1}\) is nilpotent, since this space is an equivariant quotient of \(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathbb{C}}^j(\mathfrak{m}_B/\mathfrak{m}_B^2)\) with its derivation action. The finite filtration by powers of \(\mathfrak{m}_B\) therefore shows that \(\delta\) acts nilpotently on \(B/\mathfrak{m}_B^N\) for every \(N\). Choose \(N\) such that \(\mathfrak{m}_B^N\subseteq\mathfrak{m}_BJ_{\mathrm{can}}\). The endomorphism \(T_1\) is induced on a \(\delta\)-stable subquotient of \(B/\mathfrak{m}_B^N\), so it is nilpotent.

The natural surjection
 
\[
 \Omega_B^2\otimes_B\mathbb{C}
 \to (J_{\mathrm{can}}\eta)/\mathfrak{m}_B(J_{\mathrm{can}}\eta)
\]
 
commutes with Lie differentiation. Under the identification
 
\[
 \Omega_B^2\otimes_B\mathbb{C}
 \simeq\bigwedge_{\mathbb{C}}^2(\mathfrak{m}_B/\mathfrak{m}_B^2),
\]
 
the Lie derivative is the derivation action induced by the nilpotent endomorphism on the cotangent space. It is therefore nilpotent, and so is its quotient \(T_2\).

Nakayama's lemma gives \(J_{\mathrm{can}}/\mathfrak{m}_BJ_{\mathrm{can}}\ne 0\). Taking traces yields
 
\[
 0=\operatorname{tr}(T_2)-\operatorname{tr}(T_1)
 =a(0)\dim_{\mathbb{C}}(J_{\mathrm{can}}/\mathfrak{m}_BJ_{\mathrm{can}}).
\]
 
Hence \(a(0)=0\).

Consequently, if \(\operatorname{div}_\eta\delta\) is a unit, then the induced endomorphism of \(\mathfrak{m}_B/\mathfrak{m}_B^2\) is nonnilpotent. The analytic criterion of Scheja--Wiebe~\cite[Satz~(3.1)]{SchejaWiebe1980} now gives quasi-homogeneity; see also Wahl~\cite[\S3.16]{Wahl1985}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:strict-residue}
Let \((\widetilde{V},0)\) be a Gorenstein normal complex surface singularity that is not quasi-homogeneous, put \(B:=\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{V},0}\), and let a finite group \(G\) act on \((\widetilde{V},0)\). Choose a generator \(\eta\) of \(\omega_B\) satisfying \(g\cdot\eta=\kappa(g)\eta\) for every \(g\in G\). Then
 
\[
 \dim(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}})_\kappa\geq 1.
\]
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The singularity \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is not a rational double point. Let \(p\colon(Y,F)\to(\widetilde{V},0)\) be its minimal good resolution. Put \(Z:=-\operatorname{div}_Y(p^*\eta)\) and \(D:=Z-F\). By Wahl~\cite[Lemma~3.6]{Wahl1985}, \(Z\geq F\), so \(D\geq 0\).

\emph{The case \(D\ne 0\).} Recall that \(\mathcal{Q}=\omega_B/d\Omega_B^{[1]}\) and that \(I_{\log}\) is the image of \((p_*\omega_Y(F))_0\) in \(\mathcal{Q}\). Contraction with \(\eta\) gives a \(G\)-equivariant isomorphism
 
\[
 \operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_\kappa
 \xrightarrow{\sim}\Omega_B^{[1]}.
\]
 
Moreover,
 
\[
 (p_*\omega_Y(F))_0=(p_*\mathcal{O}_Y(-D))_0\eta.
\]
 
Thus there is an isomorphism of \(G\)-representations
 
\begin{equation*}                           
 \mathcal{Q}/I_{\log}\simeq
 \frac{B}{\operatorname{div}_\eta(\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B))+(p_*\mathcal{O}_Y(-D))_0}
 \otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_\kappa.
\end{equation*}
 
Here the denominator is a complex subspace of \(B\). Since \(g\cdot\eta=\kappa(g)\eta\), Lie differentiation gives
 
\[
 \operatorname{div}_\eta(g\cdot\delta)
 =g\cdot\operatorname{div}_\eta\delta.
\]
 
Hence the denominator is \(G\)-stable.

Proposition~\ref{prop:unit-divergence} gives \(\operatorname{div}_\eta(\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B))\subseteq\mathfrak{m}_B\). Since \(D\) is nonzero and effective, a unit cannot vanish along \(D\), so \((p_*\mathcal{O}_Y(-D))_0\subseteq\mathfrak{m}_B\) as well. Evaluation at the origin therefore induces a \(G\)-equivariant surjection
 
\[
 \mathcal{Q}/I_{\log}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{C}_\kappa.
\]
 
Since complex representations of finite groups are semisimple and \(\mathcal{Q}/I_{\log}\) is a summand of \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}}\), we obtain
 
\[
 \dim(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}})_\kappa
 \geq\dim(\mathcal{Q}/I_{\log})_\kappa
 \geq 1.
\]

\emph{The case \(D=0\).} Then \(Z=F\), so \(p^*\eta\) is a nowhere vanishing section of \(\omega_Y(F)\) with character \(\kappa\). Adjunction gives
 
\[
 \omega_F\simeq\mathcal{O}_F\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_\kappa.
\]
 
Since \(F\) is connected, proper, and reduced, \(H^0(F,\mathcal{O}_F)=\mathbb{C}\). Consequently,
 
\[
 W_F\simeq\mathbb{C}_\kappa.
\]

Let \(n_i\) denote the number of intersections of \(F_i\) with the other components, counted with multiplicity. Restricting \(\omega_Y(F)\) to \(F_i\) gives
 
\[
 2g(F_i)-2+n_i=0.
\]
 
Connectedness therefore implies that \(F\) is either a single smooth elliptic curve or a cycle of smooth rational curves. In the first case, \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is simple elliptic and hence quasi-homogeneous; see Wahl~\cite[\S3.8]{Wahl1985}. This contradicts the hypothesis.

In the rational-cycle case, every \(H^0(F_i,\omega_{F_i})\) is zero. The injection of Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-one-forms} therefore gives \(\mathcal{P}=0\). Thus the summand \(W_F/\mathcal{P}\) of \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}}\) is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{C}_\kappa\), proving the assertion.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:qh-quotient-descent}
Let \((\widetilde{V},0)\) be a quasi-homogeneous Gorenstein normal complex surface singularity that is not a rational double point, and let a finite group \(H\) act on \((\widetilde{V},0)\). Then the quotient \((V,0):=(\widetilde{V},0)/H\) admits a good \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
The singularity \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is not a cyclic quotient singularity, since a Gorenstein cyclic quotient singularity is a rational double point. By M\"{u}ller~\cite[\S2, Theorem~1]{Mueller}, after conjugating \(H\) by an analytic automorphism, we may assume that \(H\) is contained in a maximal reductive algebraic subgroup of \(\operatorname{Aut}(\widetilde{V},0)\). By M\"{u}ller~\cite[\S2, Theorem~2 and Remark~(iii)]{Mueller}, the identity component of this subgroup is the central \(\mathbb{C}^*\) defining a good action. Hence this action commutes with \(H\).

Put \(B:=\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{V},0}\) and \(A:=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}=B^H\). As in the proof of M\"{u}ller's Theorem~2, choose homogeneous coordinates in which the maximal reductive group acts linearly and the defining equations are weighted homogeneous. Let \(R\) be the resulting positively graded coordinate ring, with \(R_0=\mathbb{C}\). The action of \(H\) preserves each graded piece, so
 
\[
 R^H=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}R_n^H.
\]
 
This invariant algebra is finitely generated, has degree-zero part \(\mathbb{C}\), and has only positive degrees otherwise. The finite quotient gives
 
\[
 \mathcal{O}_{(\operatorname{Spec}(R^H))^{\mathrm{an}},0}
 \simeq B^H=A.
\]
 
Thus the positive grading defines a good \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action on \((V,0)\).
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:strict-base}
Let \((V,0)\) be a normal complex surface singularity which is not quasi-homogeneous. If \((V,0)\) is Gorenstein, then \(\Delta(V,0) \geq 2\). If \((V,0)\) is non-Gorenstein and \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein, then \(\Delta(V,0) \geq 1\).
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Put \(A:=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}\). Suppose first that \((V,0)\) is Gorenstein. Since it is not quasi-homogeneous, it is not a rational double point. Its canonical cover is trivial, so \(B=A\), \(G=\{1\}\), and \(\kappa=1\). Equations~\eqref{eq:uniform-nonADE} and~\eqref{eq:Hm-class}, together with Proposition~\ref{prop:strict-residue}, give
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)
 =1+\dim\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}}
 =1+\dim\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}}
 \geq 2.
\]
 

Suppose now that \((V,0)\) is non-Gorenstein and \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. Let \(q\colon(\widetilde{V},0) \to (V,0)\) be its canonical cover, with covering group \(G\) and canonical character \(\kappa\), and put \(B:=\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{V},0}\). Then \(\kappa\neq 1\). If \(\widetilde{V}\) is smooth at the origin or \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is a rational double point, the quotient presentation \eqref{eq:quotient-cover} shows that scalar multiplication on \(\mathbb{C}^2\) induces a good \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action on \((V,0)\). This contradicts the hypothesis. Thus \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is singular and is not a rational double point. If it were quasi-homogeneous, Lemma~\ref{lem:qh-quotient-descent} would imply that \((V,0)\) is quasi-homogeneous. Hence \((\widetilde{V},0)\) is not quasi-homogeneous.

Since \(\kappa\neq 1\), equations~\eqref{eq:uniform-nonADE} and~\eqref{eq:Hm-class}, together with Proposition~\ref{prop:strict-residue}, give
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)
 =\dim(\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}})_\kappa
 =\dim(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{res}})_\kappa
 \geq 1. \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Put \(A=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}\), and let \(q\colon(\widetilde{V},0) \to (V,0)\) be the canonical cover, with local ring \(B=\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{V},0}\), covering group \(G\) and canonical character \(\kappa\). We use \(\Delta(A)=\Delta(V,0)\). If \(A\) is Gorenstein, then \(B=A\), \(G=\{1\}\), and \(\kappa=1\). Suppose first that \(B\) is singular and is not a rational double point. By Theorem~\ref{thm:uniform},
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)=\Delta(A)=\delta_{\kappa,1}
                 +\dim(\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}})_\kappa
 \geq \varepsilon(V,0),
\]
 
since \(\delta_{\kappa,1}=\varepsilon(V,0)\). If \(A\) is quasi-homogeneous, its good action lifts to \(B\) by Lemma~\ref{lem:graded-canonical-cover}, and Corollary~\ref{cor:qh-residue-zero} gives \(\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}}=0\). Thus equality holds. Conversely, Corollary~\ref{cor:strict-base} gives \(\Delta(A) \geq \varepsilon(V,0)+1\) whenever \(A\) is not quasi-homogeneous.

If \(B\) is smooth or a rational double point and \(G\) is nontrivial, Section~\ref{sec:quotient-covers} presents \(A\) as a finite linear quotient of the plane and gives \(\Delta(A)=0\). The canonical character is nontrivial, so \(\varepsilon(V,0)=0\), and scalar multiplication on the plane makes \(A\) quasi-homogeneous. Finally, if \(G\) is trivial, the singularity \(A=B\) is a rational double point, and Proposition~\ref{prop:ADE-zero} gives \(\Delta(A)=0\).
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
For a singular canonical cover other than a rational double point, the difference between the lower bounds \(1\) and \(0\) is the contribution of the trivial summand \(T_B\) to the \(\kappa\)-isotypic component. The role of a trivial summand in distinguishing the two bounds already appears in Wahl's hypersurface quotient calculation~\cite[proof of Theorem~5.2]{Wahl2015}.
