Here it is realized by the explicit quotient of two-forms defining \(T_B\), together with the residue representation, for general canonical covers without a smoothing hypothesis. Quasi-homogeneity makes the entire residue representation vanish by Euler contraction. In the other direction, failure of quasi-homogeneity supplies a nonzero canonical-character quotient by Proposition~\ref{prop:strict-residue}.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:QG-conjecture}
For a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing \(\pi\) of a non-Gorenstein normal surface singularity \((V,0)\),
 
\[
 1+\mu_\pi \geq \tau_\pi,
\]
 
with equality if and only if \((V,0)\) is quasi-homogeneous.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Since \(\pi\) is a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing, the central singularity \((V,0)\) is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. It is non-Gorenstein by assumption, so Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives \(\Delta(V,0) \ge 0\), with equality if and only if \((V,0)\) is quasi-homogeneous. Since \(\alpha_\pi=0\) by Wahl~\cite[Lemma~5.1]{Wahl2015}, Equation~\eqref{eq:introduction-wahl-smoothing} reads \(\Delta(V,0)=1+\mu_\pi-\tau_\pi\). Both assertions now follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:rational-conjecture}
For a rational surface singularity which is not a rational double point,
 
\[
 h^1(X,L_X) \ge h^1(X,S_X)
\]
 
with equality if and only if the singularity is quasi-homogeneous.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
A rational Gorenstein surface singularity is a rational double point, by Artin~\cite[pp.~134--136]{Artin1966}. Thus the hypotheses imply that \((V,0)\) is non-Gorenstein. It is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein, as recalled in Section~\ref{qg:sec:relative-cover}, so Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, together with \(h^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0\), proves the inequality and its equality criterion.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{genus:thm:main}
For every normal complex surface singularity \((V,0)\),
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)+4p_g(V,0) \ge 0
\]
 
with equality if and only if \((V,0)\) is rational and quasi-homogeneous.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{genus:lem:variation}
Let \(\pi\colon(X,E) \to (V,0)\) be a good resolution of a normal complex surface singularity, let \(F\) be a vector bundle of rank \(s\) on \(X\), and let \(N\) be a numerically trivial line bundle on \(X\). Then
 
\[
 |h^1(F)-h^1(F\otimes N)| \le s p_g,
\]
 
where \(p_g=h^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\).
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Choose an effective exceptional cycle \(H\) such that \(\mathcal{O}_X(-H)\) is relatively ample. By relative Serre vanishing, a sufficiently large multiple \(D\) of \(H\) satisfies
 
\[
 H^1(X,F(-D))=H^1(X,F\otimes N(-D))=0.
\]
 
Together with the coherent \(H^2\)-vanishing in \eqref{eq:coherent-vanishing}, the restriction sequences give isomorphisms
 
\[
 H^1(X,F)\simeq H^1(D,F|_D),\quad
 H^1(X,F\otimes N)\simeq H^1(D,(F\otimes N)|_D).
\]
 
The same vanishing makes \(H^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X) \to H^1(D,\mathcal{O}_D)\) surjective, so \(h^1(D,\mathcal{O}_D)\le p_g\).

Put \(\mathcal{G}:=\omega_D\otimes(F|_D)^\vee\), and let \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{G}\) be the image of the evaluation map
 
\[
 H^0(D,\mathcal{G})\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathcal{O}_D \to \mathcal{G}.
\]
 
Then \(H^0(D,\mathcal{A})=H^0(D,\mathcal{G})\). Since \(\mathcal{O}_D(-H)\) is ample, \(D\) is projective, and GAGA allows us to work with algebraic coherent sheaves on \(D\). At the generic point of a component of multiplicity \(m\), the local ring of \(D\) is a discrete valuation ring modulo the \(m\)th power of a uniformizer. A submodule of a free module of rank \(s\) over this principal Artinian local ring is generated by at most \(s\) elements. Thus \(s\) general linear combinations of the global sections generate \(\mathcal{A}\) at that generic point. The failure of generation is a proper algebraic condition on their complex coefficients. Since there are only finitely many components, the sections can be chosen to generate at all generic points simultaneously.

We obtain a map \(\mathcal{O}_D^{\oplus s} \to \mathcal{A}\) with finite-length cokernel. Since coherent sheaves on \(D\) have vanishing second cohomology, the cohomology sequences for its kernel and image give
 
\[
 h^1(D,\mathcal{A}) \le s h^1(D,\mathcal{O}_D).
\]
 

Tensoring a coherent sheaf on \(D\) by \(N^{-1}|_D\) preserves its Euler characteristic. Indeed, a filtration by sheaves on the reduced components and finite-length sheaves reduces this assertion to Riemann--Roch on each smooth component, where the change is the rank times \(\deg(N^{-1}|_C)=0\); see the Stacks Project~\cite[Tag~0AYV]{Stacks}. Since \(\mathcal{A}\otimes N^{-1}|_D\) is a subsheaf of \(\mathcal{G}\otimes N^{-1}|_D\), it follows that
 
\begin{align*}
 h^0(D,\mathcal{G})-h^0(D,\mathcal{G}\otimes N^{-1}|_D)
 &\le h^0(D,\mathcal{A})-h^0(D,\mathcal{A}\otimes N^{-1}|_D)\\
 &=h^1(D,\mathcal{A})-h^1(D,\mathcal{A}\otimes N^{-1}|_D)\\
 &\le s h^1(D,\mathcal{O}_D) \le s p_g.
\end{align*}
 
The cycle \(D\) is a Cartier divisor in the smooth surface \(X\), hence a Gorenstein curve. Serre duality and the restriction isomorphisms identify the left side with \(h^1(F)-h^1(F\otimes N)\). Applying the same argument to \(F\otimes N\) and \(N^{-1}\) proves the opposite inequality.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{genus:lem:strict}
Let \((X,E) \to (V,0)\) be a good resolution of a normal complex surface singularity, and let \(N\) be a numerically trivial line bundle on \(X\). If \(p_g=0\), then \(h^1(N)=0\). If \(p_g>0\), then
 
\[
 h^1(N) \le 2p_g-1.
\]
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
If \(p_g=0\), Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:variation}, applied to \(\mathcal{O}_X\) and \(N\), gives \(h^1(N)=0\). Suppose that \(p_g>0\), and put \(n:=h^1(N)\). There is nothing to prove if \(n=0\). Assume that \(n>0\). As in the restriction argument of Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:variation}, choose an effective exceptional cycle \(D\) with \(h^1(D,N|_D)=n\), having minimal sum of coefficients among all such cycles. In particular, \(D\neq 0\).

Put \(\mathcal{G}:=\omega_D\otimes N^{-1}|_D\). We adapt the minimality argument in Konno~\cite[Lemma~3.1(2)]{Konno2008} to this twisted dualizing sheaf. For every reduced irreducible component \(C\le D\), adjunction gives
 
\[
 0 \to \omega_{D-C}\otimes N^{-1}|_{D-C}
 \to \mathcal{G}
 \to \omega_C(D-C)\otimes N^{-1}|_C
 \to 0.
\]
 
The first term is understood to be zero when \(D-C=0\). If the induced restriction map on global sections were zero, this sequence and Serre duality would give
 
\[
 h^1(D-C,N|_{D-C})
 =h^0(D-C,\omega_{D-C}\otimes N^{-1}|_{D-C})
 =h^0(D,\mathcal{G})
 =n,
\]
 
contrary to the minimality of \(D\).

The kernels of these restriction maps are therefore proper linear subspaces of \(H^0(D,\mathcal{G})\). Choose a section outside their finite union. Its restriction to each reduced component is nonzero, so its coefficient in a local trivialization is a unit at every generic point of \(D\). Since \(D\) is a Cartier divisor in the smooth surface \(X\), it is Cohen--Macaulay and has no embedded associated points. The section is consequently a nonzerodivisor and gives an exact sequence
 
\[
 0 \to \mathcal{O}_D \to \mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{T} \to 0,
\]
 
where \(\mathcal{T}\) has finite length. Hence
 
\[
 h^1(D,\mathcal{G})\le h^1(D,\mathcal{O}_D).
\]
 

Numerical triviality preserves the Euler characteristic under tensoring by \(N^{-1}|_D\), as in the preceding proof. Thus Serre duality gives
 
\[
 \chi(\mathcal{G})=\chi(\omega_D)=-\chi(\mathcal{O}_D).
\]
 
It follows that
 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 n
 &=h^0(D,\mathcal{G})=\chi(\mathcal{G})+h^1(D,\mathcal{G})\\
 &\le -\chi(\mathcal{O}_D)+h^1(D,\mathcal{O}_D)=2h^1(D,\mathcal{O}_D)-h^0(D,\mathcal{O}_D)\\
 &\le 2p_g-1.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
 
Here \(h^1(D,\mathcal{O}_D)\le p_g\) follows from the restriction sequence and \eqref{eq:coherent-vanishing}, while \(h^0(D,\mathcal{O}_D)\ge 1\) because \(D\neq 0\).
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{genus:lem:euler}
Let \((Y,F)\) be a good resolution of a normal complex surface singularity or of a smooth surface point, with \(F\neq\varnothing\). Let a finite group \(G\) act on \(Y\), preserving \(F\), and let \(D\) be a \(G\)-invariant integral exceptional divisor. Define
 
\[
 C_D^\bullet:=
 [\mathcal{O}_Y(D) \xrightarrow{d} \Omega_Y^1(\log F)(D)
 \xrightarrow{d} \omega_Y(F+D)].
\]
 
The cohomology groups of its global-section complex,
 
\[
 B^i:=H^i(\Gamma(Y,C_D^\bullet)),
\]
 
are finite dimensional, and
 
\begin{equation}\label{genus:eq:euler}
 \sum_{i=0}^2(-1)^i[H^1(Y,C_D^i)]
 =[B^0]-[B^1]+[B^2]
 \quad\text{in }R(G).
\end{equation}
 
Moreover, \(B^0\) is the trivial representation when \(D\ge 0\), and is zero otherwise.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Exterior differentiation preserves the indicated pole orders in a logarithmic basis, so \(C_D^\bullet\) is a complex of sheaves of complex vector spaces. Choose a \(G\)-invariant effective exceptional cycle \(Z\ge F\) such that \(-Z\le D\). By Lemma~\ref{lem:negative-log}, \(C_{-Z}^\bullet\) resolves \(j_!\mathbb{C}_{Y\setminus F}\), where \(j\colon Y\setminus F\hookrightarrow Y\). On a sufficiently small resolution neighborhood, \(Y\) retracts onto \(F\). Thus the exact sequence
 
\[
 0 \to j_!\mathbb{C}_{Y\setminus F}
 \to \mathbb{C}_Y
 \to \mathbb{C}_F
 \to 0
\]
 
gives \(\mathbb{H}^k(Y,C_{-Z}^\bullet)=0\) for every \(k\).

Put
 
\[
 \mathcal{T}:=\mathcal{O}_Y(D)/\mathcal{O}_Y(-Z).
\]
 
The quotient complex \(C_D^\bullet/C_{-Z}^\bullet\) has terms \(\mathcal{T}\otimes\bigwedge^i\Omega_Y^1(\log F)\), all supported on the proper exceptional curve. For a \(G\)-equivariant coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{M}\) with such support, write
 
\[
 \chi_G(\mathcal{M}):=[H^0(Y,\mathcal{M})]-[H^1(Y,\mathcal{M})].
\]
 
We show that
 
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^2(-1)^i
 \chi_G(\mathcal{T}\otimes\bigwedge^i\Omega_Y^1(\log F))=0.
\]
 

Let \(G_i\) be the stabilizer of a component \(F_i\), and let \(P_i\) be the reduced divisor of its intersections with the other components. The residue sequence
 
\[
 0 \to \Omega_{F_i}^1(\log P_i)
 \to \Omega_Y^1(\log F)|_{F_i}
 \to \mathcal{O}_{F_i}
 \to 0
\]
 
is \(G_i\)-equivariant, with the natural linearization on the quotient. Taking determinants gives
 
\[
 \bigwedge^2(\Omega_Y^1(\log F)|_{F_i})
 \simeq \Omega_{F_i}^1(\log P_i)
\]
 
equivariantly. Tensoring the residue sequence by any \(G_i\)-equivariant coherent sheaf on \(F_i\) therefore makes the alternating cohomology classes of the three exterior powers cancel. Induction from \(G_i\) to \(G\) gives the same cancellation on the orbit of \(F_i\).

The corresponding cancellation also holds for sheaves of finite length. At a smooth point of \(F\), the residue map gives a trivial quotient of the logarithmic cotangent fiber. At a node with local equation \(xy=0\), the point stabilizer permutes the classes of \(d\log x\) and \(d\log y\) in that fiber. Indeed, changes of the local equations by units contribute regular differentials, whose classes in the logarithmic cotangent fiber are zero. The sum of the two classes is therefore invariant. In both cases the fiber contains a trivial summand, so its alternating exterior-power class is zero. A filtration by powers of the maximal ideal gives the same cancellation for every equivariant sheaf of finite length.

A power of the ideal of \(F\) annihilates \(\mathcal{T}\). The resulting equivariant filtration reduces the calculation to coherent sheaves on the reduced curve \(F\). The normalization map is equivariant, and its comparison with a coherent sheaf has kernel and cokernel of finite length supported at the nodes. The component and point calculations above therefore prove the asserted cancellation. Comparing the quotient complex with the acyclic complex \(C_{-Z}^\bullet\), we obtain finite-dimensional hypercohomology groups and
 
\[
 \sum_k(-1)^k[\mathbb{H}^k(Y,C_D^\bullet)]=0.
\]
 

By \eqref{eq:coherent-vanishing}, the hypercohomology spectral sequence
 
\[
 E_1^{p,q}=H^q(Y,C_D^p)
 \ \Rightarrow\ \mathbb{H}^{p+q}(Y,C_D^\bullet)
\]
 
has only the rows \(q=0,1\). The second row consists of finite-dimensional spaces, and \(E_2^{p,0}=B^p\). The only possible higher differential is \(d_2\colon E_2^{0,1}\to E_2^{2,0}\), whose source is finite dimensional. Since the abutment is finite dimensional, every \(B^p\) is finite dimensional as well. Comparing Euler characteristics gives
 
\[
 0
 =\sum_{p=0}^2(-1)^p[B^p]
 -\sum_{p=0}^2(-1)^p[H^1(Y,C_D^p)],
\]
 
which proves \eqref{genus:eq:euler}.

Finally, a meromorphic function with zero differential is constant. A nonzero constant is a section of \(\mathcal{O}_Y(D)\) exactly when \(D\ge 0\), and \(G\) acts trivially on constants.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{genus:lem:cycle}
Let \((Y,F) \to (V,0)\) be the minimal good resolution of a numerically Gorenstein normal complex surface singularity. If \((V,0)\) is a rational double point, then \(Z_K=0\). Otherwise, \(Z_K\ge F\).
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
If \((V,0)\) is a rational double point, its minimal good resolution is crepant, so \(Z_K=0\). Suppose that \((V,0)\) is not a rational double point. Let \(p\colon Y\to Y_0\) be the morphism to the minimal resolution, and let \(F_0\) be its reduced exceptional divisor. By the projection formula, \(Z_{K,0}:=p_*Z_K\) is the numerical anticanonical cycle on \(Y_0\), and it is integral. Popescu-Pampu--Seade~\cite[Proposition~2.4]{PopescuPampuSeade2009} gives
 
\[
 Z_{K,0}\ge F_0.
\]
 

Make the reduced exceptional divisor simple normal crossings by successively blowing up points where this condition fails. Consider one such blowup \(b\colon T'\to T\), with center \(x\) and new exceptional curve \(C_{\mathrm{new}}\). Suppose that the numerical anticanonical cycle before the blowup is \(Z=\sum_i z_iC_i\), with every \(z_i\ge 1\). Since \(K_{T'}=b^*K_T+C_{\mathrm{new}}\), the new numerical anticanonical cycle is
 
\[
 Z'=b^*Z-C_{\mathrm{new}}.
\]
 
Its coefficient along \(C_{\mathrm{new}}\) is
 
\[
 \sum_i z_i\operatorname{mult}_x(C_i)-1
 \ge \sum_i\operatorname{mult}_x(C_i)-1
 \ge 1.
\]
 
The last inequality holds because the reduced exceptional divisor is not simple normal crossings at \(x\), so its multiplicity there is at least two. The coefficients on the strict transforms remain unchanged. Thus the numerical anticanonical cycle remains at least the reduced exceptional divisor throughout this process.

The resulting good resolution dominates \(Y\). By the projection formula, its numerical anticanonical cycle pushes forward to \(Z_K\), with unchanged coefficients on the components that remain. Hence \(Z_K\ge F\).
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{genus:lem:closed-restriction}
Let \(\pi\colon(Y,F)\to(V,0)\) be a \(G\)-equivariant good resolution of a normal complex surface singularity, where \(G\) is finite, and let \(D\) be a \(G\)-invariant integral exceptional divisor. Let \((Y_0,F_0)\to(V,0)\) be the minimal good resolution. For the complex \(C_D^\bullet\) of Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:euler}, restriction of closed one-forms induces a \(G\)-equivariant injection
 
\[
 H^1(\Gamma(Y,C_D^\bullet))
 \hookrightarrow H^0(F_0,\omega_{F_0}).
\]
 
For a resolution of a smooth surface point, the group on the left is zero.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Put \(B^1:=H^1(\Gamma(Y,C_D^\bullet))\), and let \(p\colon Y\to Y_0\) be the natural morphism. Uniqueness of the minimal good resolution gives the induced \(G\)-action on \(Y_0\) and makes \(p\) equivariant. A class in \(B^1\) is represented by a closed meromorphic one-form \(\alpha\) on \(Y\), holomorphic off \(F\). By van Straten--Steenbrink~\cite[Corollary~(1.4)]{VanStratenSteenbrink1985}, its restriction to the punctured surface extends to a holomorphic one-form \(\alpha_0\) on \(Y_0\); see also J\"{o}rder~\cite[Proposition~1.2]{JorderExtension}. The extension is unique and remains closed, since its exterior derivative vanishes off \(F_0\). Moreover, \(p^*\alpha_0=\alpha\), since the two forms agree off \(F\).

Every section of \(\mathcal{O}_Y(D)\) restricts to a holomorphic function on the punctured normal surface and extends across the singular point. Its pullback to \(Y_0\) is constant on \(F_0\), so its differential restricts to zero on every component of \(F_0\). Thus restriction is well defined on \(B^1\). The restrictions of \(\alpha_0\) to the components are regular one-forms. Their residues at the preimages of every node are zero, so they satisfy the residue compatibility condition defining \(\omega_{F_0}\). We obtain a map
 
\[
 B^1\to H^0(F_0,\omega_{F_0}).
\]
 
Uniqueness of extension and naturality of restriction make this map equivariant.

Suppose that the image of \([\alpha]\) is zero. Then \(\alpha_0\) restricts to zero on every component of \(F_0\). As in the period argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-one-forms}, loops in \(F_0\) can be represented by piecewise smooth paths lying in its components. All their integrals are zero, including those arising from cycles in the dual graph. Since a sufficiently small resolution neighborhood retracts onto \(F_0\), all periods of \(\alpha_0\) vanish. It therefore has a global holomorphic primitive on \(Y_0\). Normality gives \((\pi_0)_*\mathcal{O}_{Y_0}=\mathcal{O}_V\), where \(\pi_0\colon Y_0\to V\), so this primitive descends to a holomorphic function \(f\) on \(V\).

Put \(h:=\pi^*(f-f(0))\). Then \(\alpha=dh\). If \(h=0\), the assertion follows immediately. Otherwise, \(h\) has positive order along every exceptional component. Let \(C\) be a component on which \(D\) has coefficient \(-a<0\). Near a general point of \(C\), choose coordinates with \(C=(x=0)\), and write \(h=x^m u\), where \(m>0\) and \(u\) is a unit. The coefficient of \(dx/x\) in \(dh\) is
 
\[
 x^m(mu+x\partial_xu),
\]
 
which has order exactly \(m\) along \(C\). Since \(dh\in H^0(Y,\Omega_Y^1(\log F)(D))\), this coefficient must vanish to order at least \(a\). Hence \(m\ge a\). This holds for every component with a negative coefficient in \(D\), so \(h\in H^0(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y(D))\). Consequently \([\alpha]=0\) in \(B^1\).

If \((V,0)\) is smooth, Hartogs extension gives a holomorphic closed one-form on a sufficiently small ball in \(V\). The holomorphic Poincar\'{e} lemma gives a primitive there. The same vanishing-order calculation on \(Y\) shows that its pullback, after subtracting its value at the origin, belongs to \(H^0(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y(D))\). Thus \(B^1=0\).
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{genus:prop:polar}
Let \(\pi\colon(Y,F)\to(V,0)\) be a \(G\)-equivariant good resolution of a numerically Gorenstein normal complex surface singularity, where \(G\) is finite. Then the class
 
\[
 [H^1(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y(Z_K-F))]
 -[H^1(Y,\Omega_Y^1(\log F)(Z_K-F))]
 +[H^1(Y,\omega_Y(Z_K))]
\]
 
is effective in \(R(G)\). The same assertion holds for a resolution of a smooth surface point.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
If \(F=\varnothing\), all three cohomology groups vanish by Stein vanishing. Suppose that \(F\neq\varnothing\). Put \(D:=Z_K-F\), and write
 
\[
 B^i:=H^i(\Gamma(Y,C_D^\bullet))
\]
 
for the cohomology groups of the global-section complex in Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:euler}. Let \(\pi_0\colon(Y_0,F_0)\to(V,0)\) be the minimal good resolution, and let \(p\colon Y\to Y_0\) be the natural morphism. If \((V,0)\) is smooth, take \(Y_0=V\) and \(F_0=\varnothing\). The morphism \(p\) is equivariant. Put \(W:=H^0(F_0,\omega_{F_0})\), with \(W=0\) when \(F_0=\varnothing\). By Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:closed-restriction}, \(B^1\) injects equivariantly into \(W\).

If \((V,0)\) is smooth or a rational double point, then \(W=0\), so \(B^1=0\). Equation~\eqref{genus:eq:euler} expresses the class in the statement as \([B^0]+[B^2]\), which is effective.

Suppose now that \((V,0)\) is neither smooth nor a rational double point. Let \(Z_{K,0}\) be the numerical anticanonical cycle on \(Y_0\). By Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:cycle}, \(Z_{K,0}\ge F_0\). The transformation formula for numerical anticanonical cycles gives
 
\[
 Z_K=p^*Z_{K,0}-K_{Y/Y_0}.
\]
 
Together with the canonical bundle formula, this yields an isomorphism
 
\[
 \omega_Y(Z_K)\simeq p^*\omega_{Y_0}(Z_{K,0})
\]
 
of \(G\)-equivariant line bundles. Since \(Z_{K,0}\ge F_0\), pullback followed by projection to cohomology defines a map \(H^0(Y_0,\omega_{Y_0}(F_0))\to B^2\). Define
 
\[
 \mathcal{J}:=\operatorname{im}\left(
 H^0(Y_0,\omega_{Y_0}(F_0))\to B^2
 \right).
\]
 

Adjunction and Grauert--Riemenschneider vanishing~\cite{GrauertRiemenschneider1970} give the equivariant exact sequence
 
\[
 0\to H^0(Y_0,\omega_{Y_0})
 \to H^0(Y_0,\omega_{Y_0}(F_0))
 \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Res}} W
 \to 0.
\]
 
If a logarithmic two-form has zero image in \(B^2\), its pullback is the differential of a one-form in \(H^0(Y,\Omega_Y^1(\log F)(D))\). On the punctured surface this primitive is holomorphic. Lemma~\ref{lem:exact-residue}, applied on \(Y_0\), therefore shows that the logarithmic two-form has zero residue. Consequently residue descends to a well-defined equivariant surjection
 
\[
 \operatorname{Res}\colon\mathcal{J}\twoheadrightarrow W.
\]
 

Identify \(B^1\) with its image in \(W\). The inclusions \(\mathcal{J}\subseteq B^2\) and \(B^1\subseteq W\), together with the residue surjection, give
 
\[
 [B^0]-[B^1]+[B^2]
 =[B^0]+[B^2/\mathcal{J}]
 +[\ker(\operatorname{Res})]+[W/B^1].
\]
 
Every term on the right is the class of a finite-dimensional \(G\)-representation. Hence the class is effective, and \eqref{genus:eq:euler} proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{genus:lem:cyclic-log-cover}
Let \(\pi\colon(X,E) \to (V,0)\) be a good resolution of a normal complex surface singularity, or a resolution of a smooth surface point. Put \(U:=X\setminus E\), and let \(c\colon U' \to U\) be a connected finite unramified cyclic cover with group \(G\).

Then \(c\) extends to a finite cyclic cover \(\tau\colon(V',0') \to (V,0)\), unramified away from \(0\). There are a \(G\)-equivariant good resolution \(\pi'\colon(Y,F) \to (V',0')\) and a map \(q\colon Y \to X\) satisfying \(\pi\circ q=\tau\circ\pi'\). The map \(q\) factors as \(q=\rho\circ\sigma\), where \(\rho\colon\overline{X} \to X\) is the finite normalization in \(U'\), and \(\sigma\colon Y \to \overline{X}\) is a \(G\)-equivariant toroidal resolution.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
If \(E=\varnothing\), then \(X\) is a sufficiently small smooth neighborhood of the origin. The connected cover is trivial, and we take all maps to be identities. Assume that \(E\ne\varnothing\). Choose a sufficiently small representative of \((V,0)\). Its punctured neighborhoods retract onto the link, so the connected cover remains connected after further shrinking.

The complement of \(E\) in a small coordinate neighborhood has fundamental group \(\mathbb{Z}\) at a smooth point of \(E\), and \(\mathbb{Z}^2\) at a node. Each connected local component of the cover therefore extends by normalization of
 
\[
 w^m=x^a y^b,
 \quad 0\le a,b<m,
 \quad \gcd(m,a,b)=1,
\]
 
where \(m\) is the order of the local monodromy image. At a smooth point of \(E\), take \(b=0\). These normalizations glue by uniqueness of normalization to give \(\rho\colon\overline{X} \to X\). They are smooth over smooth points of \(E\), and have cyclic quotient singularities over its nodes; cf.~Esnault--Viehweg~\cite[Lemma~3.24]{EsnaultViehweg1992}. Their minimal toric resolutions give a \(G\)-equivariant toroidal resolution \(\sigma\colon Y \to \overline{X}\). Put
 
\[
 q:=\rho\circ\sigma,\quad F:=(q^{-1}E)_{\mathrm{red}}.
\]

The Stein factorization of \(\pi\circ q\) gives \(Y \xrightarrow{\pi'} V' \xrightarrow{\tau} V\), with \(V'\) normal and \(\tau\) finite. Over \(V\setminus\{0\}\), it is the cover \(U' \to U\). If \(\tau^{-1}(0)\) contained more than one point, finiteness would separate the inverse image of a sufficiently small neighborhood into disjoint neighborhoods of these points. Removing the fiber would disconnect the restricted cover, a contradiction. Thus \(\tau^{-1}(0)=\{0'\}\). The \(G\)-action descends to \(V'\), and \(\tau\) is a cyclic cover. Since \(Y\) is smooth, \(F\) has simple normal crossings, and \(\pi'\) is an isomorphism away from \(F\), the map \(\pi'\colon(Y,F) \to (V',0')\) is a good resolution.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{genus:lem:log-pullback}
For the map \(q\colon Y \to X\) constructed in Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:cyclic-log-cover}, pullback induces a \(G\)-equivariant isomorphism
 
\begin{equation}\label{genus:eq:logpullback}
 q^*\Omega_X^1(\log E) \simeq \Omega_Y^1(\log F).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Over a node of \(E\), toric coordinates give
 
\[
 x=u^a v^b,\quad y=u^c v^d,\quad ad-bc\ne 0,
\]
 
and hence
 
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}dx/x\\ dy/y\end{pmatrix}
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}du/u\\ dv/v\end{pmatrix}.
\]
 
The matrix is invertible over \(\mathbb{C}\). Where only one toric boundary coordinate vanishes, the other is a unit, and its logarithmic differential is regular. Over a smooth point of \(E\), the local map is \(x=u^m,\ y=v\). Pullback sends \(dx/x\) to \(m du/u\), and \(dy\) to \(dv\). Away from \(F\), the map is unramified. These calculations prove the isomorphism; cf.~Ambro~\cite[Theorem~1.1(b)]{Ambro2016}. It is \(G\)-equivariant because it is induced by pullback.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{genus:lem:cyclic-descent}
For the map \(q\colon Y \to X\) constructed in Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:cyclic-log-cover} and every vector bundle \(\mathcal{A}\) on \(X\), pullback induces isomorphisms
 
\begin{equation}\label{genus:eq:descent}
 H^i(X,\mathcal{A}) \simeq H^i(Y,q^*\mathcal{A})^G
 \quad(i=0,1).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Write \(q=\rho\circ\sigma\) as in Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:cyclic-log-cover}. Cyclic quotient singularities are rational; see Esnault--Viehweg~\cite[proof of Claim~5.13]{EsnaultViehweg1992}. Thus
 
\[
 \sigma_*\mathcal{O}_Y=\mathcal{O}_{\overline{X}},
 \quad R^1\sigma_*\mathcal{O}_Y=0.
\]
 
Since \(\rho\) is finite and \(X=\overline{X}/G\), it follows that
 
\[
 R^1q_*\mathcal{O}_Y=0,\quad
 (q_*\mathcal{O}_Y)^G=\mathcal{O}_X.
\]
 
The projection formula and Leray give
 
\[
 H^i(Y,q^*\mathcal{A})
 \simeq H^i(X,\mathcal{A}\otimes q_*\mathcal{O}_Y)
 \quad(i=0,1).
\]
 
The Reynolds projection identifies the invariant subsheaf on the right with \(\mathcal{A}\) and commutes with cohomology. Taking invariants therefore proves \eqref{genus:eq:descent}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{genus:lem:horizontal-section}
Let \(q\colon Y \to X\) be the map constructed in Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:cyclic-log-cover}. Let \(P\) be a line bundle on \(X\) with a flat logarithmic connection \(\nabla\) along \(E\). Suppose that the pullback connection has trivial monodromy on \(Y\setminus F\).

Then there are a \(G\)-invariant integral divisor \(D\) supported on \(F\) and a character \(\chi\) of \(G\) such that
 
\[
 (q^*P,q^*\nabla) \simeq (\mathcal{O}_Y(D),d)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_\chi
\]
 
as \(G\)-equivariant line bundles with logarithmic connection. Here \(d\) is exterior differentiation, and \(\mathbb{C}_\chi\) is the one-dimensional representation with character \(\chi\).
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:log-pullback}, the pullback connection is logarithmic along \(F\). Its trivial monodromy gives a nonzero global horizontal section \(s\) on the connected space \(Y\setminus F\).

Near a point of \(F\), choose a local frame \(e\) of \(q^*P\) and coordinates in which \(F\) is defined by \(u=0\) or \(uv=0\). Flatness gives a connection form
 
\[
 \ell_1\frac{du}{u}+\ell_2\frac{dv}{v}+dh,
\]
 
with constant residues and \(h\) holomorphic. The second logarithmic term is omitted when \(F\) has one branch. Trivial monodromy implies that the residues are integral. The horizontal equation then gives
 
\[
 s=c u^{-\ell_1}v^{-\ell_2}\exp(-h)e
\]
 
for a nonzero constant \(c\), with the \(v\)-factor omitted in the one-branch case. Thus \(s\) extends meromorphically to \(Y\), and \(D:=\operatorname{div}(s)\) is integral and supported on \(F\).

The horizontal sections on \(Y\setminus F\) form a one-dimensional vector space preserved by \(G\). Define \(\chi\) by \(g\cdot s=\chi(g)s\). Then \(D\) is \(G\)-invariant, and multiplication by \(s\) gives the equivariant identification
 
\[
 \mathcal{O}_Y(D)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_\chi
 \simeq q^*P.
\]
 
Since \(q^*\nabla(s)=0\), this identification carries exterior differentiation to \(q^*\nabla\).
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{genus:prop:twist}
Let \(\pi\colon(X,E) \to (V,0)\) be a good resolution of a normal complex surface singularity. Then there is a numerically trivial line bundle \(N\) on \(X\) such that
 
\[
 h^1(X,N)-h^1(X,S_X\otimes N)+h^1(X,L_X\otimes N) \geq 0.
\]
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Choose a positive integer \(r\) such that \(rZ_K\) is integral. The line bundle \(\omega_X^{\otimes r}(rZ_K)\) has degree zero on every exceptional component. Since \(X\) retracts onto \(E\) and \(H^2(E,\mathbb{Z})\) is freely generated by the component degree classes, its first Chern class is zero. The exponential sequence identifies the group of numerically trivial line bundles with a quotient of \(H^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\). Multiplication by \(r\) is surjective on this quotient. Hence there is a numerically trivial line bundle \(N\) such that
 
\[
 N^{\otimes r} \simeq \omega_X^{\otimes r}(rZ_K).
\]

Put \(P:=L_X\otimes N\). Since \(L_X\simeq\omega_X^\vee(-E)\), we have
 
\[
 P^{\otimes r} \simeq \mathcal{O}_X(r(Z_K-E)).
\]
 
Transport the exterior-differentiation connection to \(P^{\otimes r}\) through this isomorphism. Dividing its local connection forms by \(r\) defines a flat logarithmic connection \(\nabla\) on \(P\). Indeed, the connection forms on \(P^{\otimes r}\) change by \(r\) times the logarithmic differentials of the transition functions of \(P\). The \(r\)th tensor power of \((P,\nabla)\) is trivial as a flat line bundle on \(U:=X\setminus E\), so its monodromy is finite.

Let \(U' \to U\) be the connected cover corresponding to the kernel of this monodromy representation. Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:cyclic-log-cover} gives a good resolution \(\pi'\colon(Y,F) \to (V',0')\), a map \(q\colon Y \to X\), and a covering group \(G\). The pullback connection has trivial monodromy on \(Y\setminus F\). By Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:horizontal-section}, there are a \(G\)-invariant integral divisor \(D\) supported on \(F\) and a character \(\chi\) such that
 
\[
 (q^*P,q^*\nabla)
 \simeq (\mathcal{O}_Y(D),d)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_\chi.
\]
 
The natural rank-two identity
 
\[
 L_X\otimes\Omega_X^1(\log E)\simeq S_X
\]
 
and the logarithmic pullback isomorphism \eqref{genus:eq:logpullback} give the following \(G\)-equivariant identifications:
 
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 q^*(L_X\otimes N)
 &\simeq \mathcal{O}_Y(D)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_\chi,\\
 q^*(S_X\otimes N)
 &\simeq \Omega_Y^1(\log F)(D)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_\chi,\\
 q^*N
 &\simeq \omega_Y(F+D)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_\chi.
 \end{aligned}
\]

The line bundle \(q^*N\) is numerically trivial: each exceptional curve on \(Y\) maps either to an exceptional curve on \(X\) or to a point. The last identification therefore gives
 
\[
 (K_Y+F+D)\cdot C=0
\]
 
for every exceptional component \(C\) on \(Y\). By uniqueness of the numerical anticanonical cycle,
 
\[
 Z_{K,Y}=F+D.
\]
 
This cycle is integral, so \((V',0')\) is numerically Gorenstein, or is a smooth surface point.

Proposition~\ref{genus:prop:polar}, together with the three identifications above, shows that
 
\[
 [H^1(Y,q^*(L_X\otimes N))]
 -[H^1(Y,q^*(S_X\otimes N))]
 +[H^1(Y,q^*N)]
 \in R(G)
\]
 
is effective. Here tensoring by \(\mathbb{C}_\chi\) preserves effectivity. Taking \(G\)-invariants and applying Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:cyclic-descent} gives
 
\[
 h^1(X,L_X\otimes N)-h^1(X,S_X\otimes N)+h^1(X,N)
 \geq 0,
\]
 
as required.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Let \(\pi\colon(X,E) \to (V,0)\) be the minimal good resolution, and put \(p_g:=p_g(V,0)=h^1(\mathcal{O}_X)\). Choose \(N\) as in Proposition~\ref{genus:prop:twist}, and define
 
\[
 \Delta_N:=h^1(N)-h^1(S_X\otimes N)+h^1(L_X\otimes N).
\]
 
Then \(\Delta_N\geq 0\).

Applying Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:variation} to \(S_X\) and \(L_X\), of ranks \(2\) and \(1\), respectively, gives
 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 \Delta(V,0)+4p_g
 &=\Delta_N+5p_g-h^1(N)\\
 &\quad+h^1(S_X\otimes N)-h^1(S_X)\\
 &\quad+h^1(L_X)-h^1(L_X\otimes N)\\
 &\geq\Delta_N+2p_g-h^1(N).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
 
If \(p_g=0\), Lemma~\ref{genus:lem:strict} gives \(h^1(N)=0\), so \(\Delta(V,0)\geq\Delta_N\geq 0\). If \(p_g>0\), the same lemma gives \(h^1(N)\leq 2p_g-1\), and therefore
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)+4p_g\geq\Delta_N+1\geq 1.
\]
 
Thus the inequality holds in all cases, and equality forces \(p_g=0\).

The condition \(p_g=0\) is equivalent to rationality. For a rational singularity other than a rational double point, Theorem~\ref{thm:rational-conjecture} gives \(\Delta(V,0)=0\) if and only if \((V,0)\) is quasi-homogeneous. A rational double point is rational and quasi-homogeneous, and Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives \(\Delta(V,0)=0\).
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{prop:depth}
For every \(i \in \mathbb{Z}\),
 
\[
 C_i \simeq \ker(t:H^2_{\mathfrak{m}_R}(M_i)
 \to H^2_{\mathfrak{m}_R}(M_i)),
 \delta_i=0 \Longleftrightarrow \operatorname{depth}_R M_i=3.
\]
 
In particular, \(\delta_0=\delta_1=0\).
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Since \(N_i\) has depth two, local cohomology of \eqref{eq:specialization} gives \(C_i \simeq H^1_{\mathfrak{m}_A}(M_i/tM_i)\). The sequence \(0 \to M_i \xrightarrow{t} M_i \to M_i/tM_i \to 0\) identifies this group with the displayed kernel. The regular-element criterion gives \(\operatorname{depth}_R M_i=\operatorname{depth}_A(M_i/tM_i)+1\), so \(C_i=0\) is equivalent to depth three. Finally, \(M_0=R\) and \(M_1=\omega_R\) are maximal Cohen--Macaulay.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{prop:duality}
For every \(i \in \mathbb{Z}\),
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:duality}
 \delta_i=\delta_{1-i}.
\end{equation}
 
In particular,
 
\begin{equation*}                 
 \alpha_\pi=\delta_{-1}=\delta_2.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
The module \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(M_i,\omega_R)\) has finite length, since \(M_i\) is invertible off the closed point. Reflexivity and canonical duality in codimension one give \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_i,\omega_R)=M_{1-i}\). Change of rings gives
 
\[
 \operatorname{Ext}^{q+1}_R(M_i/tM_i,\omega_R)
 \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(M_i/tM_i,\omega_A) (q \ge 0).
\]
 
Dualizing \eqref{eq:specialization} over \(A\), and using the Cohen--Macaulay property of \(N_i\), gives
 
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{Hom}_A(M_i/tM_i,\omega_A)=N_{1-i},\\
 \operatorname{Ext}^1_A(M_i/tM_i,\omega_A)=\operatorname{Ext}^2_A(C_i,\omega_A)=D_A(C_i),
 \end{gathered}
\]
 
where \(D_A\) denotes Matlis duality. Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,\omega_R)\) to \(0 \to M_i \xrightarrow{t} M_i \to M_i/tM_i \to 0\) therefore gives
 
\[
 0 \to C_{1-i} \to \operatorname{Ext}^1_R(M_i,\omega_R) \xrightarrow{t} \operatorname{Ext}^1_R(M_i,\omega_R) \to D_A(C_i) \to 0.
\]
 
Here \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_R(M_i,\omega_R)=0\) by local duality and \(\operatorname{depth}_R M_i \ge 2\). The kernel and cokernel of multiplication by \(t\) on \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(M_i,\omega_R)\) have equal lengths, and Matlis duality preserves length. This proves \eqref{eq:duality}.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:rr}
Let \(\pi\) be a one-parameter smoothing of a rational normal complex surface singularity. With \(n,K,Z_i,u_i\) as above, for every \(i\in\mathbb{Z}\) we have
 
\begin{align}
 \delta_i
 &=\frac12\left[i(i-1)(\mu_\pi-n)+(2i-1)KZ_i+Z_i^2\right]
 \label{eq:rr-expanded}\\
 &=\frac{u_i(u_i-K)}2+\binom{i}{2}(\mu_\pi-n-K^2).
 \label{eq:rr}
\end{align}
 
Both expressions are independent of the resolution on which the full pullback is invertible.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
By Steenbrink~\cite[Theorem~1]{Steenbrink1995}, the smoothing extends, preserving the parameter, to a flat projective family \(g\colon\mathcal{Y} \to T\). After shrinking \(T\), the central fiber \(Y_0\) has the given singularity as its only singular point, and \(g\) is smooth elsewhere. The sheaf \(\omega_{\mathcal{Y}/T}^{[i]}\) is torsion-free over the smooth curve \(T\), and hence flat over \(T\). Its restriction to a smooth fiber is \(\omega_{Y_t}^{\otimes i}\). Constancy of its fiberwise Euler characteristic and the specialization sequence \eqref{eq:specialization} give
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:euler}
 \delta_i
 =\chi(Y_0,\omega_{Y_0}^{[i]})
 -\chi(Y_t,\omega_{Y_t}^{\otimes i}).
\end{equation}

Extend the chosen local resolution to a projective resolution \(p\colon\overline{X} \to Y_0\), and write
 
\[
 \overline{\mathscr{L}}_i
 :=p^*(\omega_{Y_0}^{[i]})/\mathrm{torsion}.
\]
 
Its restriction near the exceptional divisor is \(\mathscr{L}_i\). Pullback of sections and reflexive extension across the singular point give \(p_*\overline{\mathscr{L}}_i\simeq\omega_{Y_0}^{[i]}\). Over an affine neighborhood of that point, relative generation gives an exact sequence
 
\[
 0 \to \mathscr{G}
 \to \mathcal{O}_{\overline{X}}^{\oplus m}
 \to \overline{\mathscr{L}}_i
 \to 0.
\]
 
Rationality gives \(R^1p_*\mathcal{O}_{\overline{X}}=0\), and the fiber dimension gives \(R^2p_*\mathscr{G}=0\). Thus
 
\begin{equation*}                          
 p_*\overline{\mathscr{L}}_i
 \simeq\omega_{Y_0}^{[i]},
 \quad R^1p_*\overline{\mathscr{L}}_i=0.
\end{equation*}
 
Consequently,
 
\[
 \chi(Y_0,\omega_{Y_0}^{[i]})
 =\chi(\overline{X},\overline{\mathscr{L}}_i).
\]
 
Rationality and flatness also give
 
\[
 \chi(\overline{X},\mathcal{O}_{\overline{X}})
 =\chi(Y_0,\mathcal{O}_{Y_0})
 =\chi(Y_t,\mathcal{O}_{Y_t}).
\]

The exceptional divisor is a tree of \(n\) rational curves, so \(e(E)=n+1\). By Greuel--Steenbrink~\cite{GreuelSteenbrink1983}, the Milnor fiber has \(b_1(M_\pi)=0\). It has the homotopy type of a finite complex of dimension at most two, and hence \(e(M_\pi)=1+\mu_\pi\). Comparing a resolution neighborhood with the Milnor fiber gives
 
\[
 e(\overline{X})-e(Y_t)=n-\mu_\pi.
\]
 
Noether's formula therefore yields
 
\[
 K_{\overline{X}}^2-K_{Y_t}^2=\mu_\pi-n.
\]

The canonical identification away from \(E\) gives
 
\[
 \overline{\mathscr{L}}_i
 \simeq\mathcal{O}_{\overline{X}}(iK_{\overline{X}}+Z_i).
\]
 
Applying Riemann--Roch to \(\overline{X}\) and \(Y_t\) in \eqref{eq:euler}, we obtain
 
\[
 \delta_i
 =\frac12\left[
 i(i-1)(K_{\overline{X}}^2-K_{Y_t}^2)
 +(2i-1)K_{\overline{X}}Z_i+Z_i^2
 \right].
\]
 
Since \(Z_i\) is exceptional, the definition of the numerical canonical cycle gives \(K_{\overline{X}}Z_i=KZ_i\). Substitution proves \eqref{eq:rr-expanded}. Expanding \(u_i=iK+Z_i\) then gives \eqref{eq:rr}.

Let \(b\colon X' \to X\) be a blowup at a point of \(E\), with exceptional curve \(C\). The full line bundle on \(X'\) is \(b^*\mathscr{L}_i\), so
 
\[
 u_i'=b^*u_i,\quad K'=b^*K+C,\quad n'=n+1.
\]
 
Since \(C^2=-1\) and \(C\) is orthogonal to pullbacks,
 
\[
 n'+(K')^2=n+K^2,\quad
 u_i'(u_i'-K')=u_i(u_i-K).
\]
 
Any two resolutions on which the full pullback is invertible admit a common resolution by point blowups. Thus \eqref{eq:rr}, and consequently \eqref{eq:rr-expanded}, is independent of the chosen resolution.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:periodic}
Let \(\pi\) be a one-parameter smoothing of a rational normal complex surface singularity \((V,0)\) of canonical index \(r>1\), and put \(A:=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}\). There are rational numbers \(\gamma_i(A)\), depending only on \(A\), such that
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:periodic}
 \delta_i(\pi)
 =\binom{i}{2}(\mu_\pi-n-K^2)+\gamma_i(A)
 \quad(i\in\mathbb{Z}).
\end{equation}
 
They satisfy
 
\[
 \gamma_{i+r}(A)=\gamma_i(A),\quad
 \gamma_i(A)=\gamma_{1-i}(A),\quad
 \gamma_0(A)=\gamma_1(A)=0.
\]
 
Consequently,
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:period-shift}
\begin{aligned}
 \delta_r(\pi)
 &=\binom{r}{2}(\mu_\pi-n-K^2),\quad
 \mu_\pi\geq n+K^2,\\
 \delta_{i+r}(\pi)-\delta_i(\pi)
 &=\left(ri+\frac{r(r-1)}2\right)(\mu_\pi-n-K^2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Choose a common resolution on which the full pullbacks of \(\omega_A^{[j]}\), for \(0\leq j<r\), are invertible. The local isomorphisms \(\omega_A^{[i+r]}\simeq\omega_A^{[i]}\) identify their full pullbacks, so \(u_{i+r}=u_i\). Define
 
\[
 \gamma_i(A):=\frac{u_i(u_i-K)}2.
\]
 
The blowup calculation in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:rr} shows that this number is independent of the resolution. It depends only on \(A\), and the equality \(u_{i+r}=u_i\) gives its \(r\)-periodicity. Theorem~\ref{thm:rr} gives \eqref{eq:periodic}.

Lemma~\ref{prop:depth} gives \(\delta_0=\delta_1=0\), so \eqref{eq:periodic} implies \(\gamma_0=\gamma_1=0\). Lemma~\ref{prop:duality} and the identity \(\binom{1-i}{2}=\binom{i}{2}\) then give \(\gamma_i=\gamma_{1-i}\).

Taking \(i=r\) in \eqref{eq:periodic} gives the formula for \(\delta_r\). Since \(\delta_r\geq 0\) and \(\binom{r}{2}>0\), it follows that \(\mu_\pi\geq n+K^2\). Finally, subtracting \eqref{eq:periodic} for \(i\) from the same formula for \(i+r\), and using
 
\[
 \binom{i+r}{2}-\binom{i}{2}
 =ri+\frac{r(r-1)}2,
\]
 
proves \eqref{eq:period-shift}.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:finite}
Let \(\pi\colon(\mathcal{V},0) \to (T,0)\) be a smoothing of a normal complex \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein surface singularity \((V,0)\) of canonical index \(r>1\). Then \(\pi\) is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein if and only if \(\delta_i(\pi)=0\) for every \(2 \le i \le r\). When these conditions hold, the total space \((\mathcal{V},0)\) has canonical index \(r\), every \(M_i\) is maximal Cohen--Macaulay, and the natural restriction maps
 
\[
 M_i/tM_i \to N_i
 \quad(i \in \mathbb{Z})
\]
 
are isomorphisms.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Recall that \(R=\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{V},0}\), \(A=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}=R/(t)\), \(M_i=\omega_R^{[i]}\), and \(N_i=\omega_A^{[i]}\).

Suppose that \(\delta_i(\pi)=0\) for \(2 \le i \le r\). Since \(N_r \simeq A\), the specialization sequence \eqref{eq:specialization} gives \(M_r/tM_r \simeq A\). Lifting a generator and applying Nakayama's lemma gives a surjection \(R \to M_r\). This is an isomorphism because \(R\) is a domain and \(M_r\) has rank one. Consequently,
 
\[
 M_{i+r} \simeq M_i
 \quad(i \in \mathbb{Z}).
\]
 
By Lemma~\ref{prop:depth} and \(\delta_0=\delta_1=0\), the modules \(M_0,\ldots,M_{r-1}\) are maximal Cohen--Macaulay. Periodicity gives the same assertion for every \(M_i\). Another application of Lemma~\ref{prop:depth} shows that every specialization map is an isomorphism.

Put \(s:=\operatorname{index}(R)\). Since \(M_r \simeq R\), we have \(s \mid r\). Conversely, a trivialization of \(M_s\) restricts to a trivialization of the \(s\)th canonical power on \(V\setminus\{0\}\). Reflexive extension gives \(N_s \simeq A\), so \(r \mid s\). Thus \(s=r\).

Let \(q\colon(\widetilde{V},0) \to (V,0)\) be the canonical cover defined by a chosen trivialization \(N_r \simeq A\), and put \(B:=\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{V},0}\). Choose a trivialization \(M_r \simeq R\) inducing this trivialization on the central fiber. Such a choice is possible because units of \(A\) lift to units of \(R\). Form the cyclic algebra
 
\[
 \widetilde{R}:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r-1}M_i.
\]
 
Its grading defines an action of \(G:=\mu_r\), with \(t\) invariant and \(\widetilde{R}^G=R\). The specialization isomorphisms identify \(\widetilde{R}/t\widetilde{R}\) with \(B\) as a \(G\)-equivariant algebra: compatibility with multiplication holds on the punctured central surface and extends by reflexivity.

The finite \(R\)-algebra \(\widetilde{R}\) is local because its quotient by \(t\) is local. It is Cohen--Macaulay because each summand \(M_i\) is maximal Cohen--Macaulay over \(R\). Since \(t\) is a nonzerodivisor and \(B\) is Gorenstein, \(\widetilde{R}\) is Gorenstein. Away from the closed point, \(R\) is regular and the cyclic cover is locally defined by \(z^r=u\), with \(u\) a unit. It is therefore \'{e}tale there. Thus \(\widetilde{R}\) is regular in codimension one and is normal by Serre's criterion. It is flat over \(T\), and its nonzero fibers are \'{e}tale covers of the smooth fibers of \(\pi\). Hence it defines the required \(G\)-equivariant smoothing of \((\widetilde{V},0)\).

Conversely, suppose that \(\pi\) is induced by a \(G\)-equivariant smoothing \(\widetilde{\pi}\colon(\widetilde{\mathcal{V}},0) \to (T,0)\) of the canonical cover, with trivial action on \(T\). Put \(\widetilde{R}:=\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{V}},0}\). Since \(\widetilde{R}/t\widetilde{R} \simeq B\) and \(t\) is a nonzerodivisor, \(\widetilde{R}\) is normal and Gorenstein. Every nonidentity element of \(G\) fixes only the origin on the central fiber. Its fixed locus in \(\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}\) therefore has dimension at most one near the origin. Consequently, the quotient map is \'{e}tale in codimension one.

Choose an eigen-generator \(\eta\) of \(\omega_{\widetilde{R}}\). Equivariant adjunction identifies its character with the canonical character \(\kappa\) of \(B\), since \(t\) is invariant. On the locus where the quotient map is \'{e}tale, multiplication by \(\eta^{\otimes i}\) and descent identify the \(\kappa^{-i}\)-eigensummand of \(\widetilde{R}\) with \(M_i\).

A system of parameters of \(R\) is also a system of parameters of \(\widetilde{R}\). Since \(\widetilde{R}\) is Cohen--Macaulay, it is maximal Cohen--Macaulay as an \(R\)-module. Its eigensummands are direct summands and have the same property. They are therefore reflexive, so the preceding identifications extend across the complement of the \'{e}tale locus. Thus every \(M_i\) is maximal Cohen--Macaulay, and Lemma~\ref{prop:depth} gives \(\delta_i(\pi)=0\) for every \(i \in \mathbb{Z}\).
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:short-finite-criterion}
Canonical duality reduces the list of vanishing conditions: \(\pi\) is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein if and only if \(\delta_r=0\) and \(\delta_j=0\) for \(2 \le j \le \lceil r/2\rceil\). Indeed, the proof of Proposition~\ref{thm:finite} shows that \(\delta_r=0\) gives \(M_{i+r} \simeq M_i\) and \(\delta_{i+r}=\delta_i\). Lemma~\ref{prop:duality} then gives \(\delta_j=\delta_{r+1-j}\) for \(2 \le j<r\). The second range is empty when \(r=2\).
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:numerical}
Let \((V,0)\) be a rational normal complex surface singularity of canonical index \(r>1\), and put \(A:=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}\). A smoothing \(\pi\) of \((V,0)\) is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein if and only if
 
\[
 \mu_\pi=n+K^2,\quad
 \gamma_j(A)=0
 \quad(2 \le j<r).
\]
 
If \(r=2\), then
 
\[
 \delta_i(\pi)=\binom{i}{2}(\mu_\pi-n-K^2)
 \quad(i \in \mathbb{Z}),
\]
 
and \(\pi\) is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein if and only if \(\mu_\pi=n+K^2\).
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Corollary~\ref{cor:periodic} gives
 
\[
 \delta_r(\pi)=\binom{r}{2}(\mu_\pi-n-K^2),\quad
 \delta_j(\pi)=\binom{j}{2}(\mu_\pi-n-K^2)+\gamma_j(A)
 \quad(2 \le j<r).
\]
 
Since \(r>1\), the equality \(\delta_r(\pi)=0\) is equivalent to \(\mu_\pi=n+K^2\). Under this equality, the remaining conditions \(\delta_j(\pi)=0\) for \(2 \le j<r\) are precisely \(\gamma_j(A)=0\). Proposition~\ref{thm:finite} therefore proves the first assertion.

If \(r=2\), periodicity and \(\gamma_0(A)=\gamma_1(A)=0\) give \(\gamma_i(A)=0\) for every \(i \in \mathbb{Z}\). Substitution in \eqref{eq:periodic} gives the displayed formula for \(\delta_i(\pi)\), and the first assertion gives the stated criterion.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:weak-numerical}
Let \(\pi\colon(\mathcal{V},0) \to (T,0)\) be a smoothing of a rational normal complex surface singularity \((V,0)\) of canonical index \(r>1\). The canonical divisor \(K_{\mathcal{V}}\) of the total space is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Cartier if and only if \(\mu_\pi=n+K^2\). When these conditions hold, \((\mathcal{V},0)\) has canonical index \(r\).
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Recall that \(R=\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{V},0}\), \(A=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}=R/(t)\), \(M_i=\omega_R^{[i]}\), and \(N_i=\omega_A^{[i]}\).

Suppose that \(\mu_\pi=n+K^2\). Corollary~\ref{cor:periodic} gives \(\delta_r(\pi)=0\). Since \(N_r \simeq A\), the specialization sequence \eqref{eq:specialization} gives \(M_r/tM_r \simeq A\). Lifting a generator and applying Nakayama's lemma gives a surjection \(R \to M_r\). This is an isomorphism because \(R\) is a domain and \(M_r\) has rank one. Thus \(K_{\mathcal{V}}\) is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Cartier.

Put \(s:=\operatorname{index}(R)\). The isomorphism \(M_r \simeq R\) gives \(s \mid r\). A trivialization of \(M_s\) restricts to a trivialization of the \(s\)th canonical power on \(V\setminus\{0\}\). Reflexive extension gives \(N_s \simeq A\), so \(r \mid s\). Consequently, \(s=r\).

Conversely, suppose that \(K_{\mathcal{V}}\) is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Cartier, and let \(s\) be the canonical index of \(R\). The same restriction argument gives \(r \mid s\). Since \(M_s \simeq R\), Lemma~\ref{prop:depth} gives \(\delta_s(\pi)=0\). Periodicity and \(r \mid s\) give \(\gamma_s(A)=\gamma_0(A)=0\). Hence Corollary~\ref{cor:periodic} yields
 
\[
 0=\delta_s(\pi)=\binom{s}{2}(\mu_\pi-n-K^2).
\]
 
Since \(s \ge r>1\), it follows that \(\mu_\pi=n+K^2\).
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:canonical-specialization-representation}
The \emph{canonical-specialization representation} of \(\pi\) is the finite-dimensional complex \(G\)-representation
 
\[
 \mathcal{C}_\pi:=\operatorname{coker}\varphi,
\]
 
with the action induced by the specialization homomorphism of the compatible canonical algebras.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:canonical-specialization-representation}
With the notation above, the specialization homomorphism gives an exact sequence of \(G\)-equivariant \(A\)-modules
 
\[
 0 \to \widetilde{R}/t\widetilde{R} \xrightarrow{\varphi} B \to \mathcal{C}_\pi \to 0.
\]
 
The \(\kappa^{-j}\)-eigenspace of \(\mathcal{C}_\pi\) is the cokernel \(C_j\) in \eqref{eq:specialization}, and
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:canonical-specialization-representation}
 [\mathcal{C}_\pi]=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\gamma_j(A)[\mathbb{C}_{\kappa^{-j}}]
 \quad\text{in }R(G).
\end{equation}
 
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(\pi\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein;
\item \(\mathcal{C}_\pi=0\);
\item \(\widetilde{R}\) is Cohen--Macaulay;
\item \(\gamma_j(A)=0\) for every \(j\in\mathbb{Z}\).
\end{enumerate}
In the last condition, it suffices to take \(2\leq j<r\).
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:weak-numerical} gives \(\mu_\pi=n+K^2\). Corollary~\ref{cor:periodic} therefore gives \(\delta_j(\pi)=\gamma_j(A)\) for every \(j\), and in particular \(\delta_r=0\). Thus \(M_r/tM_r \to N_r\) is an isomorphism. A chosen trivialization of \(N_r\) lifts to one of \(M_r\), since units of \(A\) lift to units of \(R\). This gives compatible multiplications on the two cyclic algebras.

Take the direct sum of the specialization sequences \eqref{eq:specialization} for \(0\leq j<r\). The resulting injection is compatible with multiplication on the punctured central fiber. It is therefore an algebra homomorphism everywhere, since \(B\) is torsion-free over \(A\). In the canonical grading, the summands \(M_j\) and \(N_j\) have character \(\kappa^{-j}\), as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{thm:finite}. Its cokernel is consequently the direct sum of the \(C_j\) with these characters. Each \(C_j\) has finite length, and its complex dimension is \(\delta_j(\pi)=\gamma_j(A)\). This proves \eqref{eq:canonical-specialization-representation}. The character \(\kappa\) has order \(r\), so these are all the distinct irreducible characters of \(G\).

By Lemma~\ref{prop:depth}, \(\mathcal{C}_\pi=0\) if and only if every \(M_j\), for \(0\leq j<r\), is maximal Cohen--Macaulay over \(R\). Their direct sum is \(\widetilde{R}\). Since the finite local extension \(R\subseteq\widetilde{R}\) has dimension three, a system of parameters of \(R\) is also a system of parameters of \(\widetilde{R}\). Thus this module condition is equivalent to \(\widetilde{R}\) being Cohen--Macaulay. Since \(\delta_r=0\), Proposition~\ref{thm:finite} identifies the same vanishing with the strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein condition. Finally, the \(r\)-periodicity of \(\gamma_j(A)\) and \(\gamma_0(A)=\gamma_1(A)=0\) give the remaining equivalence and the shorter range. \qedhere
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{ex:lem:invariant-curve}
Let \(\zeta\) be a primitive cube root of unity, put \(E_\zeta:=\mathbb{C}/(\mathbb{Z}+\mathbb{Z}\zeta)\) and \(S:=E_\zeta\times E_\zeta\), and let \(G:=\langle g\rangle\) act by \(g(x,y)=(\zeta x,\zeta y)\). There exists a smooth connected \(G\)-invariant ample curve \(C \subset S\) containing all nine fixed points, with
 
\[
 C/G \simeq \mathbb{P}^1,\quad
 g(C)=7,\quad C^2=12.
\]
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Let \(b\colon\widehat{S} \to S\) be the blowup of the nine fixed points. By Roulleau--Urz\'{u}a~\cite[Proposition~3.1]{RoulleauUrzua2015}, the quotient \(Y:=\widehat{S}/G\) is the blowup of \(\mathbb{P}^2\) at the twelve triple points of the dual Hesse arrangement. The quotient map is branched over the strict transforms of its nine lines.

Let \(\ell \subset Y\) be the strict transform of a general plane line. Its inverse image \(\widehat{C}\) is a smooth connected triple cover of \(\ell \simeq \mathbb{P}^1\), totally ramified at nine points. Riemann--Hurwitz gives
 
\[
 2g(\widehat{C})-2=3(-2)+9(3-1)=12.
\]
 
Moreover, \(\widehat{C}^2=3\), and \(\widehat{C}\) meets each exceptional curve of \(b\) transversely at one point. Consequently, \(C:=b(\widehat{C})\) is smooth, contains all nine fixed points, and satisfies \(C^2=3+9=12\). Its quotient is \(\ell\), and its genus is seven. An irreducible curve of positive square on an abelian surface is ample.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:weak-qg}
There exists a weighted homogeneous rational normal complex surface singularity \((V,0)\) of canonical index three admitting a weakly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing \(\pi\) whose total space has a rational singularity at the origin, with
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)=0,\quad \mu_\pi=3,\quad
 \alpha_\pi=2,\quad \tau_\pi=6.
\]
 
Thus \(1+\mu_\pi-\tau_\pi=-2\), so the strong hypothesis in Theorem~\ref{thm:QG-conjecture} cannot be replaced by the weak condition.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Choose \(\zeta,S,G,C\) as in Lemma~\ref{ex:lem:invariant-curve}, and put \(L:=\mathcal{O}_S(C)\). We use the action \(g\cdot\alpha=(g^{-1})^*\alpha\). Write \(\mathbb{C}_{\zeta^j}\) for the one-dimensional representation on which \(g\) acts by multiplication by \(\zeta^j\).

\emph{Construction of the smoothing.} Give \(L\) its divisor linearization, so that the section \(f\) defining \(C\) is invariant. Define the graded algebras
 
\[
 \mathscr{B}:=\bigoplus_{d \ge 0}H^0(S,L^d),\quad
 \mathscr{R}:=\mathscr{B}^G,\quad
 \mathscr{A}:=\mathscr{R}/(f).
\]
 
Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be the complex analytic space associated with \(\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{R}\), and put \(V:=\{f=0\} \subset \mathcal{V}\). At the vertices, write
 
\[
 R:=\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{V},0},\quad
 A:=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}=R/(f).
\]
 
The punctured section cone is identified with the complement of the zero section in \(\operatorname{Tot}(L^{-1})\); see Watanabe~\cite[\S1]{Watanabe1981}. At a fixed point of \(S\), choose an eigen-equation \(z\) of \(C\) and a fiber coordinate \(w\) on \(L^{-1}\). Then
 
\[
 g\cdot z=\zeta^2z,\quad
 g\cdot w=\zeta w,\quad f=zw.
\]
 
Thus \(G\) acts freely on the punctured cone. For \(f\ne 0\), the fiber coordinate is determined by the base point, and the fiber is isomorphic to \((S\setminus C)/G\). In particular, every nonzero fiber is smooth. Since \(\mathscr{R}\) is torsion-free over \(\mathbb{C}[f]\), the map \(\pi:=f\colon(\mathcal{V},0) \to (\mathbb{C},0)\) is flat.

\emph{Normality and rationality.} Kodaira vanishing and Serre duality give
 
\[
 H^1(S,L^d)=0\quad(d\ne 0),\quad
 H^1(S,\mathcal{O}_S)=\mathbb{C}_{\zeta}^{\oplus2},\quad
 H^2(S,\mathcal{O}_S)=\mathbb{C}_{\zeta^2}.
\]
 
Put \(L_C:=L|_C\) and \(T_C:=\bigoplus_{d \ge 0}H^0(C,L_C^d)\). The restriction sequences give
 
\[
 0 \to \mathscr{B}/(f) \to T_C
 \to H^1(S,\mathcal{O}_S) \to 0,
\]
 
where the last term is concentrated in degree one. Taking invariants gives \(\mathscr{A}\simeq T_C^G\). The full section ring \(T_C\) is normal, so \(A\) is normal. Its positive grading defines a good \(\mathbb{C}^*\)-action.

Set \(Z:=\operatorname{Tot}(L^{-1})\). Since \(Z \to S\) is affine,
 
\[
 H^j(Z/G,\mathcal{O}_{Z/G})
 \simeq
 \left(\bigoplus_{d \ge 0}H^j(S,L^d)\right)^G
 =0\quad(j>0).
\]
 
The contraction \(Z/G \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{R}\) is proper and birational. The singularities of \(Z/G\) are cyclic quotient singularities and hence rational. Resolving them preserves the displayed cohomology groups. Since \(\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{R}\) is affine, the higher direct images of the structure sheaf of this resolution vanish. Thus \((\mathcal{V},0)\) is rational.

For the central curve, we have
 
\[
 H^1(C,\mathcal{O}_C)^G=0,\quad
 H^1(C,L_C)\simeq H^2(S,\mathcal{O}_S)
 =\mathbb{C}_{\zeta^2}.
\]
 
The first equality follows from \(C/G\simeq\mathbb{P}^1\), and the second follows from the restriction sequence for \(L\). For \(d\ge 2\), Serre duality gives \(H^1(C,L_C^d)=0\), since \(\deg L_C=12=2g(C)-2\). Consequently,
 
\[
 H^1(\operatorname{Tot}(L_C^{-1})/G,
 \mathcal{O}_{\operatorname{Tot}(L_C^{-1})/G})
 \simeq
 \left(\bigoplus_{d \ge 0}H^1(C,L_C^d)\right)^G
 =0.
\]
 
Resolving the cyclic quotient singularities and applying the same contraction argument proves that \((V,0)\) is rational.

\emph{Canonical powers and specialization.} Let \(\mathscr{B}_j\) be the character-\(\zeta^j\) summand of \(\mathscr{B}\), for \(j\in\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}\). Watanabe~\cite[Theorem~2.8]{Watanabe1981} identifies the canonical module with
 
\[
 \omega_{\mathscr{B}}
 \simeq \mathscr{B}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}_{\zeta}.
\]
 
Indeed, a nonzero holomorphic two-form on \(S\) has character \(\zeta\), and the logarithmic differential in the fiber direction has trivial character. Canonical descent therefore gives
 
\[
 \omega_{\mathscr{R}}\simeq\mathscr{B}_2,\quad
 \omega_{\mathscr{R}}^{[2]}\simeq\mathscr{B}_1,\quad
 \omega_{\mathscr{R}}^{[3]}\simeq\mathscr{R}.
\]
 
These identifications also hold after passage to analytic local rings. The canonical character has order three, and an eigenunit has trivial character upon evaluation at the vertex. Thus \(R\) has canonical index three.

Restriction to the punctured central surface and reflexive extension show that the canonical index of \(A\) divides three. It cannot be one: if \(A\) were Gorenstein, Gorensteinness would lift across the regular element \(f\) in the Cohen--Macaulay ring \(R\). Hence \(A\) also has index three.

Put \(\mathfrak{n}:=\mathscr{B}_{>0}\). By Watanabe~\cite[Proposition~2.2]{Watanabe1981},
 
\[
 (H^2_{\mathfrak{n}}(\mathscr{B}))_d
 \simeq H^1(S,L^d)
 =
 \begin{cases}
 \mathbb{C}_{\zeta}^{\oplus2},&d=0,\\
 0,&d\ne 0.
 \end{cases}
\]
 
In particular, the covering cone has depth two. Taking the character-\(\zeta\) summand computes the second local cohomology of \(\omega_{\mathscr{R}}^{[2]}\). This finite-length module is preserved by localization and flat passage to the analytic local ring. Hence
 
\[
 H^2_{\mathfrak{m}_R}(\omega_R^{[2]})
 \simeq \mathbb{C}^{\oplus2}.
\]
 
Multiplication by \(f\) raises degree by one and annihilates this module. Lemmas~\ref{prop:depth} and~\ref{prop:duality} therefore give \(\delta_2(\pi)=\alpha_\pi=2\).

\emph{Smoothing invariants.} Positive weighted dilation identifies the homotopy type of the local Milnor fiber with that of the global fiber \(f^{-1}(1)\simeq(S\setminus C)/G\). Since the action on \(S\setminus C\) is free,
 
\[
 e(M_\pi)=\frac{e(S)-e(C)}3
 =\frac{0-(-12)}3=4.
\]
 
The Gysin sequence identifies \(H^1(S\setminus C,\mathbb{Q})\) with \(H^1(S,\mathbb{Q})\), because the map \(H^0(C,\mathbb{Q}) \to H^2(S,\mathbb{Q})\) sends \(1\) to the nonzero class \([C]\). The invariant part of \(H^1(S,\mathbb{Q})\) is zero. Thus \(b_1(M_\pi)=0\). Since the Milnor fiber is Stein and has homotopy dimension at most two, \(e(M_\pi)=1+\mu_\pi\), and hence \(\mu_\pi=3\).

The singularity \((V,0)\) is quasi-homogeneous and has canonical index three, so Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives \(\Delta(V,0)=0\). Wahl's formula \eqref{eq:wahl} then gives
 
\[
 \tau_\pi=1+\mu_\pi+\alpha_\pi-\Delta(V,0)=6. \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:component-comparison}
Let \(\pi\) and \(\pi'\) be one-parameter smoothings of \((V,0)\). Then
 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:alpha-component-comparison}
\begin{aligned}
 \alpha_\pi-\alpha_{\pi'} &=\mu_\pi-\mu_{\pi'},\\
 \tau_\pi-\tau_{\pi'} &=2(\mu_\pi-\mu_{\pi'}).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

 
Consequently, two smoothing components have the same dimension if and only if they have the same Milnor number. The dimensions of all smoothing components have the same parity.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
Wahl~\cite[Proposition~2.2]{Wahl2015} expresses \(1+\mu_\pi-\alpha_\pi\) and \(\tau_\pi-2\alpha_\pi\) in terms of the cohomology and intersection numbers of the minimal good resolution of \((V,0)\). Both expressions are independent of the smoothing. Subtracting their values for \(\pi\) and \(\pi'\) gives the two equalities.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:one-qg}
Let \((V,0)\) be a rational non-Gorenstein normal complex surface singularity admitting a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing \(\pi_0\). Then every one-parameter smoothing \(\pi\) of \((V,0)\) satisfies
 
\[
 \mu_\pi \geq \mu_{\pi_0},
\]
 
with equality if and only if \(\pi\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Since \(\pi_0\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein, every \(\delta_i(\pi_0)\) vanishes. Equation~\eqref{eq:smoothing-difference} therefore gives
 
\[
 \delta_i(\pi)
 =\binom{i}{2}(\mu_\pi-\mu_{\pi_0})
 \quad(i \in \mathbb{Z}).
\]
 
Taking \(i=2\) and using \(\delta_2(\pi)\geq 0\) proves the inequality. Equality holds precisely when every \(\delta_i(\pi)\) vanishes. By Proposition~\ref{thm:finite}, this is equivalent to the strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein condition.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:weak-strong-with-smoothing}
Let \((V,0)\) be a rational non-Gorenstein normal complex surface singularity. If \((V,0)\) admits a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing, then every weakly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein one-parameter smoothing of \((V,0)\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. Consequently, a weakly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing which is not strong rules out the existence of a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing on any component.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
Choose a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing \(\pi_0\), and let \(\pi\) be weakly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. Write \(n\) for the number of exceptional components of the minimal good resolution and \(K\) for its numerical canonical cycle. Proposition~\ref{prop:weak-numerical} gives
 
\[
 \mu_\pi=n+K^2=\mu_{\pi_0}.
\]
 
Proposition~\ref{prop:one-qg} therefore shows that \(\pi\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. The last assertion is the contrapositive.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:gm-minimal-milnor}
Let \((V,0)\) be a rational non-Gorenstein normal complex surface singularity admitting a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing \(\pi_0\). Let \(\pi\colon(\mathcal{V},0)\to(T,0)\) be another one-parameter smoothing, and put \(R:=\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{V},0}\). Then \(R\) admits a Gorenstein modification in the sense of \cite{DaoIyamaTakahashiWemyss2020} if and only if \(\mu_\pi=\mu_{\pi_0}\). Under these equivalent conditions, if \(r\) is the canonical index of \((V,0)\), the algebra
 
\[
 \operatorname{End}_R\left(\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}\omega_R^{[j]}\right)
\]
 
is a Gorenstein modification of \(R\). If \(\mu_\pi>\mu_{\pi_0}\), then \(R\) admits no noncommutative crepant resolution.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
The ring \(R\) is a three-dimensional Cohen--Macaulay normal local domain with a canonical module and contains \(\mathbb{C}\). If \(R\) admits a Gorenstein modification, then \(K_R\) is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Cartier by Dao--Iyama--Takahashi--Wemyss~\cite[Theorem~3.5(2)]{DaoIyamaTakahashiWemyss2020}. Thus \(\pi\) is weakly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. Corollary~\ref{prop:weak-strong-with-smoothing} shows that \(\pi\) is strong, and Proposition~\ref{prop:one-qg} gives \(\mu_\pi=\mu_{\pi_0}\).

Conversely, suppose that \(\mu_\pi=\mu_{\pi_0}\). Proposition~\ref{prop:one-qg} shows that \(\pi\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. By Proposition~\ref{thm:finite}, \(R\) has canonical index \(r\), and its canonical cover
 
\[
 \widetilde{R}:=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}\omega_R^{[j]}
\]
 
is Gorenstein. By Dao--Iyama--Takahashi--Wemyss~\cite[Theorem~3.5(1)]{DaoIyamaTakahashiWemyss2020}, \(\operatorname{End}_R(\widetilde{R})\) is a Gorenstein modification of \(R\). Finally, every noncommutative crepant resolution is a Gorenstein modification, so the last assertion follows.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:global-qg-numerical}
Let \(Y\) be a normal projective complex surface with rational singularities \(P_1,\dotsc,P_s\), each admitting a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing of Milnor number \(\mu_i^0\). Let \(g\colon\mathcal{Y}\to T\) be a flat projective one-parameter smoothing over a smooth pointed curve \((T,0)\), with central fiber \(Y\). Write \(Y_t:=g^{-1}(t)\), and let \(\mu_i\) be the Milnor number of the induced smoothing at \(P_i\). Then, for \(t\ne0\) sufficiently close to \(0\),
 
\[
 K_Y^2-K_{Y_t}^2
 =\sum_{i=1}^s(\mu_i-\mu_i^0)\geq0.
\]
 
Equality holds if and only if \(g\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein near \(Y\). Equivalently, writing \(e\) for the topological Euler characteristic,
 
\[
 e(Y_t)\geq e(Y)+\sum_{i=1}^s\mu_i^0,
\]
 
with equality under the same condition.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
At each non-Gorenstein point \(P_i\), Proposition~\ref{prop:one-qg} gives \(\mu_i\geq\mu_i^0\), with equality precisely when the induced smoothing is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. A rational Gorenstein surface singularity is a rational double point, and every smoothing of such a point is Gorenstein with the same Milnor number. Thus the same conclusion holds at every \(P_i\).

Let \(p\colon X\to Y\) be the minimal good resolution. Write
 
\[
 K_X=p^*K_Y+\sum_{i=1}^sK_i,
\]
 
where \(K_i\) is the numerical canonical cycle supported over \(P_i\), and let \(n_i\) be the number of exceptional components over \(P_i\). The divisor \(K_Y\) is \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Cartier because the singularities of \(Y\) are rational. Proposition~\ref{prop:weak-numerical} gives \(\mu_i^0=n_i+K_i^2\) at every non-Gorenstein point. At a rational double point, \(K_i=0\) and \(\mu_i^0=n_i\). Rationality gives \(\chi(\mathcal{O}_X)=\chi(\mathcal{O}_Y)\) and \(e(X)=e(Y)+\sum_i n_i\). Since the exceptional cycles over distinct points are disjoint and orthogonal to \(p^*K_Y\), Noether's formula yields
 
\[
 12\chi(\mathcal{O}_Y)
 =K_X^2+e(X)
 =K_Y^2+e(Y)+\sum_{i=1}^s\mu_i^0.
\]
 
Flatness gives \(\chi(\mathcal{O}_{Y_t})=\chi(\mathcal{O}_Y)\), and replacement of the singular points by their Milnor fibers gives \(e(Y_t)=e(Y)+\sum_i\mu_i\). Applying Noether's formula to \(Y_t\) and subtracting proves the identity and inequalities.

Equality holds precisely when every induced local smoothing is strong. By Proposition~\ref{thm:finite}, every reflexive canonical power then specializes at the non-Gorenstein points. The same holds at the Gorenstein points and on the smooth locus. These conditions are local, and the finitely many local canonical indices have a common multiple. They therefore give the strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein condition for \(g\) near \(Y\). The converse follows by applying the same local criterion.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:qg-minimal-components}
Let \((V,0)\) be a rational non-Gorenstein normal complex surface singularity admitting a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing. A one-parameter smoothing of \((V,0)\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein if and only if its corresponding smoothing component has the smallest dimension among all smoothing components.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
Choose a strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein smoothing \(\pi_0\). By Corollary~\ref{prop:component-comparison},
 
\[
 \tau_\pi-\tau_{\pi_0}
 =2(\mu_\pi-\mu_{\pi_0})
\]
 
for every one-parameter smoothing \(\pi\). Proposition~\ref{prop:one-qg} shows that the right side is nonnegative and vanishes precisely when \(\pi\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. Since \(\tau_\pi\) is the dimension of the corresponding smoothing component, the assertion follows.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:qhd-qg}
Let \(\pi\colon(\mathcal{V},0) \to (\Delta,0)\) be a rational homology disk smoothing of a normal complex surface singularity \((V,0)\). Put \(R:=\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{V},0}\) and \(A:=\mathcal{O}_{V,0}\), and let \(t\) denote the pullback of a coordinate on \(\Delta\), so that \(A=R/(t)\). Then \(\pi\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein, and \(R\) and \(A\) have the same canonical index. For every \(i \in \mathbb{Z}\), the natural map
 
\begin{equation*}                              
 \omega_R^{[i]}/t\omega_R^{[i]} \to \omega_A^{[i]}
\end{equation*}
 
is an isomorphism, and \(\omega_R^{[i]}\) is maximal Cohen--Macaulay.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
Fix \(i \in \mathbb{Z}\), and choose a good resolution \(p\colon(X,E) \to (V,0)\) dominating the minimal good resolution, on which the full pullback of \(\omega_A^{[i]}\) is a line bundle. Write
 
\[
 E=\sum_{a=1}^n E_a,\quad
 \mathscr{L}_i \simeq \mathcal{O}_X(iK_X+Z_i),\quad
 u_i:=iK+Z_i,
\]
 
where \(Z_i\) is an integral exceptional divisor and \(K\) is the numerical canonical cycle.

By Stipsicz--Szab\'{o}--Wahl~\cite[Proposition~2.4(2), (4)]{SSW2008}, the minimal good resolution lattice embeds in a negative diagonal lattice of the same rank. Under this embedding, the numerical canonical cycle maps to an integral characteristic element, and its square is the negative of the rank. These properties persist under point blowups. Indeed, a point blowup \(b\) adds an orthogonal class \(e\) with \(e^2=-1\), and the numerical canonical cycle becomes \(b^*K+e\). Thus the chosen resolution lattice also embeds in a negative diagonal lattice of rank \(n\), in which \(K\) is integral and characteristic and \(K^2=-n\).

Choose a diagonal basis \(e_1,\dotsc,e_n\) with \(e_a\cdot e_b=-\delta_{ab}\), and write \(K=\sum_a k_a e_a\). Since \(K\) is characteristic, every \(k_a\) is odd. The equality \(K^2=-n\) gives \(\sum_a k_a^2=n\), so every \(k_a\) is \(1\) or \(-1\). Changing the signs of the basis vectors, we may assume that \(K=\sum_a e_a\).

Since \(\mu_\pi=0\) and \(K^2=-n\), Theorem~\ref{thm:rr} gives
 
\[
 \delta_i=\frac{u_i(u_i-K)}2.
\]
 
Both \(K\) and the image of \(Z_i\) are integral in the diagonal lattice. Hence \(u_i=\sum_a u_{i,a}e_a\) with \(u_{i,a} \in \mathbb{Z}\), and
 
\begin{equation*}                                   
 0 \leq \delta_i
 =-\frac12\sum_{a=1}^n u_{i,a}(u_{i,a}-1)
 \leq 0.
\end{equation*}
 
Thus \(\delta_i=0\). Since \(i\) was arbitrary, every reflexive canonical power specializes. Lemma~\ref{prop:depth} also shows that every \(\omega_R^{[i]}\) is maximal Cohen--Macaulay.

The rational singularity \((V,0)\) has finite canonical index \(r\). On its minimal good resolution, \(K^2=-n<0\), so it is not a rational double point. Since a rational Gorenstein surface singularity is a rational double point~\cite[pp.~134--136]{Artin1966}, \((V,0)\) is non-Gorenstein and \(r>1\). Proposition~\ref{thm:finite} now gives index preservation and a \(G\)-equivariant smoothing of the index-one cover.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:qhd-components}
Every normal surface singularity admitting a rational homology disk smoothing is rational and quasi-homogeneous. Every such smoothing \(\pi\) occurs over a one-dimensional smoothing component and satisfies \(\alpha_\pi=0\) and \(\Delta(V,0)=0\).
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:qhd-qg}, the smoothing is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein. Since \(\mu_\pi=0\) and a smoothing component has positive dimension, Theorem~\ref{thm:QG-conjecture} gives
 
\[
 1 \leq \tau_\pi \leq 1.
\]
 
Hence \(\tau_\pi=1\), and the equality criterion gives quasi-homogeneity. Theorem~\ref{thm:qhd-qg} and Lemma~\ref{prop:duality} give \(\alpha_\pi=\delta_{-1}=0\). Wahl's formula~\eqref{eq:wahl} therefore gives
 
\[
 \Delta(V,0)=1+\mu_\pi-\tau_\pi+\alpha_\pi=0. \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:qhd-classification}
The normal complex surface singularities admitting a rational homology disk smoothing are precisely the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the cyclic quotient singularities
 
\[
 \frac1{p^2}(1,pq-1), p>q>0, \gcd(p,q)=1;
\]
 
\item the weighted homogeneous singularities determined by the taut graphs in Bhupal--Stipsicz~\cite[Figure~1]{BhupalStipsicz2011};
\item the weighted homogeneous singularities with graphs in Bhupal--Stipsicz~\cite[Figure~2]{BhupalStipsicz2011}  with the cross ratio  \(\lambda=e^{\pm\pi i/3}\) for \((3,3,3;4)\), \(\lambda=2\) for \((2,4,4;3)\), and \(\lambda=9\) for \((2,3,6;2)\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:qhd-csrc-application}
Theorem~\ref{thm:qhd-qg} and Corollary~\ref{cor:qhd-components} show that every normal surface singularity admitting a rational homology disk smoothing is rational and weighted homogeneous with \(\Delta(V,0)=0\), and that every such smoothing \(\pi\) is strongly \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein with \(\tau_\pi=1\). The strong \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Gorenstein condition implies that the canonical-specialization representation of Proposition~\ref{prop:canonical-specialization-representation} vanishes. Expressing the vanishing of its character multiplicities in terms of the Seifert data of weighted homogeneous surface singularities and combining the resulting equations with Hodge inequalities yields explicit formulas for the Seifert data in many cases. Park--Shin~\cite{ParkShinQHD} combine these equations with the properties above and mainly algebraic-geometric arguments to recover the Bhupal--Stipsicz~\cite{BhupalStipsicz2011} classification of weighted homogeneous surface singularities admitting rational homology disk smoothings.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
